items.body: Over the course of a month-long bicycle journey across southern and central Thailand, H. Flora accumulated a personal archive of nocturnal field recordings. These recordings became the basis for two interconnected releases, each approaching the same ecosystems from a different perspective. Anthropause presents the material in its raw form: rainforests alive with gibbons, amphibian choirs, Tokay geckos, bats and insects captured during the hours when human activity had receded to its minimum. Noumenon takes those same recordings as its starting point, reshaping them through modular synthesis, electronic processing and improvisation into a “naturel-concrète” ecosystem. The relationship between the albums never feels schematic. Anthropause already demonstrates a careful compositional ear. Each lengthy piece unfolds episodically through changing densities and acoustic perspectives rather than functioning as a documentary collage. Different species occupy distinct spatial registers, creating a strong sense of internal organisation without any intervention beyond careful listening and recording. H. Flora repeatedly resists the temptation to isolate individual sounds, allowing the rainforest to remain a collective acoustic environment whose complexity exceeds immediate human understanding. That sense of immersion carries naturally into Noumenon. Here the field recordings dissolve into modular drones, fractured rhythms and densely layered electronic textures whose origins are often impossible to identify. Animal calls become synthetic oscillations before gradually revealing their biological source; electronic gestures acquire the behaviour of insects or amphibians. Nature and technology enter into a continuous exchange, with the album always remaining profoundly organic. What ultimately distinguishes these releases is the absence of ecological sentimentality. H. Flora is not constructing a fantasy of untouched wilderness, nor imagining a world cleansed of humanity. His recordings repeatedly acknowledge how difficult it has become to find moments free from anthropogenic noise, while Noumenon accepts that any attempt to imagine a post-human ecosystem remains speculative. Heard in parallel, the two albums also begin to unsettle the listener’s assumptions about sound itself. The raw recordings of Anthropause, with their hissing rainforests, reveal the mechanics of nature through high frequencies, rhythmic pulses, amphibian loops and electronic-sounding timbres, while Noumenon demonstrates how organic modular synthesis and digital processing can become when they remain attentive to those same acoustic behaviours. The boundary between documentation and invention becomes increasingly porous, exposing just how strange and sonically complex the natural world already is. Personally — and somewhat ironically — I found that, at times, Noumenon adhered more faithfully to my own imagined soundscape of a rainforest in Thailand. For this armchair traveller, H. Flora’s “Nocturnal Fantasias” may even feel more authentic than the ambience documented on Anthropause. Of course, I am exaggerating here, but this also goes to show how difficult it can be to leave one’s own expectations behind, even when embarking remotely on a sonic expedition. Across the two albums, bioacoustics and electroacoustic composition become part of the same exploratory process, beginning with the act of listening and following wherever the sounds happen to lead. Taking us on his travels, H. Flora kindly answered a few questions via email elaborating on the production process. The two releases, Anthropause and Noumenon, feel like complementary perspectives on the same material. One presents the rainforest as recorded, while the other imagines how these ecosystems might evolve in the prolonged absence of humanity. At what point did you realise that the project needed to exist in these two parallel forms rather than as a single album? Well, it was more of a fluid process than a decision. When I scanned through the original material to see what I could find and did some cutting around parts where there was subtle human activity, I realised again how challenging it was to capture sonic moments in which those sounds could really be perceived in an isolated, pure form. So, by making chops here and there, I started to extract parts that I really liked and began playing around with them. It just came naturally over time from this initial idea of capturing the sonic footprint of the non-human world, and I felt it could be extended by building something on top of that attempt. More in the sense that I could create my own individual idea of a possible version of the anthropause. The title Anthropause refers to the idea of a temporary withdrawal of human activity from the environment. During your nocturnal recordings across Thailand, were you trying to document moments where nature seemed to reclaim the acoustic foreground, or was the album also a reflection on the impossibility of ever fully removing the human presence from contemporary ecosystems? I mean, for me it is more an excercise to record in nature. It is a way to expand my own senses and to visualize how beautiful and unique it can be to get yourself into this multilayered, complex non-human world of communication and sonic order and chaos. Therefore, I need to search sometimes for the acoustic space on which i want to focus to get into this certain sphere of perception. The partly highly contrasting sounds created by humans and the quantitatively presence, its effects on the territorial behaviour of animals and therefore, among other things, on the sonic landscapes is sure something which can not be dismissed overall while recording. also myself, I am part of this ambivalent relation. we are all. So I didn’t really want to reduce the framework of these pieces on a imagination, where humankind finally vanished for its sinful, destructive nature of being and an acoustic domesticity being finally claimed again by the so called natural world and so on. I found it more fitting to see and understand it as a kind of Noumenon, something that can be measured from a certain perspective and that one has a responsibility to react to, but which, on the other hand, cannot really be perceived in its entirety; something one cannot fully understand in all its dimensions, and something that is not perceptible solely through a human understanding of things. The earthly sphere and its ecosystem have their own complex “logic”, with or without our presence. And it is also the case that the sonic stage should be allowed to belong to someone else for a change.. You spent a month travelling through Thailand by bicycle, often recording after 10 p.m. or before dawn to minimise human interference. How did those long periods of isolated listening change your relationship with environmental sound? Were there particular encounters—whether the gibbons of Phang Nga, the amphibian choirs, the Tokay geckos, or the cave-dwelling bat colonies—that fundamentally altered your understanding of these ecosystems? It was more like a last-minute trip and, in general, when I travel nowadays, I’m not really well prepared and I do it without much planning. So basically, I had absolutely no idea what to expect when I arrived there. I had got these new clip-on microphones beforehand, and my intention was to get familiar with them, play around and experiment a bit. But I quickly noticed after arriving that there was a huge sonic landscape to explore. I remember that somewhere on the coast I started making my first recordings at night, and this one animal was very close to me and had this strange, distinctive sound. So the next morning I asked some people around the bungalows and played them my recording. It was a tokay gecko, and for the locals it was more than familiar. They were giggling—it’s a well-known guy there. This kind of thing happened to me many times. I remember sitting in a small roadside restaurant at night in Khao Sok National Park and having a lot of fun talking with the owners. Then this frog began to croak. I pointed towards the sound and they immediately responded that it was the “bullfrog”, because it blows up its cheeks in order to make the sounds it does. When everything had closed down and it was late enough that there probably wouldn’t be much traffic anymore, I went back to the place and luckily the colony was still there, croaking. The next day I met a birdwatcher who told me about this Facebook group, “Thai Biodiversity Survey & Species ID”, a very active, wonderful group with a lot of professionals helping each other. From then on, I used it a lot to identify the animals and plants around me. So yeah, I learned a lot about Thailand’s highly biodiverse environment through making these recordings. The sound artist and theorist Gerald Fiebig describes your work as occupying a space between pure phonography and electroacoustic composition. How do you navigate the balance between faithfully documenting a soundscape and reshaping it into something new? Is there a point at which a field recording ceases to be documentation and becomes composition? It can also be the other way around, so that the composition is already there, recorded, and therefore gets documented. I think it always depends on how one understands it and from which angle it is observed. It can be the same as with photography or other fields of art. It is documentation. And even if it is meant to be understood as a pure composition, it is still a certain kind of documentation. But I don’t really think too much about that, to be honest. It is more of a process with a life of its own. I do not try to put that much control on it. When it feels right and attracts my energy, I go on. When there is a framework or a narrative evolving around the work, even better. On the other hand, I have plenty of recordings—for example, from Iceland last year—that I have tried to work with, but they haven’t led to any fruitful progress yet. Many passages on Noumenon blur the boundaries between natural and synthetic sound. At times it becomes difficult to distinguish an animal call from a modular synthesis process or a heavily transformed recording. What attracts you to this ambiguity, and do you see electronic manipulation as a way of extending nature’s own processes rather than imposing something artificial upon them? I think it is simply another way to play around with our possible means of (creative) expression. It always depends on how one wants to channel or expand the material and shift it into another context. I think art always has something to do with a kind of communication. And what has been chosen here is communication with a certain excerpt of the surrounding environment. Within it lies a wide aesthetic sonic palette that provides a lot of interesting material for exploration. I would say I don’t have a particular plan for those sounds. I just borrow them, shapeshift and transform them into something else, and give them back to the environment. That is the whole compositional interplay. Even so, it mostly arises from experimentation, and it isn’t as if I put a lot of focus on composition and arrangement; it’s more of an improvisational process. You cycled for 2300 km. What would you say surprised you the most that you were unable to capture or to render sonically? Suprisingly it even exceeded my expectations and I was overall happy with the results and the diversity of the recordings. But… maybe the fart of a elephant, that would have been something (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body:
Slowspin Combines Ambient-Jazz & Hindustani Folk On New Album 'AFTERIMAGE'

19 August 2026

'Afterimage', the latest album by Zeerak Ahmed aka SLOWSPIN, isn't the first time the U.S.-based Karachi-rooted artist has expressed the inner worlds of the diaspora. Her archival sound installation 'Mother, I Am Compelled to Leave' has done that before. Neither is it the first time she has combined folk influences with contemporary instrumentation. That's been done with similar themes on her previous critically lauded album 'TALISMAN'.

However, the new 10-track record sees her grip the universality in both aspects tighter and shed off the excess further with a minimalist approach. The blunt, heavy hits of drums with brushes or mallets, clean guitar strums, and sometimes harps and woodwinds too, put the work in the textural jazz palette along with its slightly improvisational nature. The simple melodies on tracks like lullaby-like 'Jaat Rahi' or the sustained longings of 'Hari Hari' add a safe consonance to the album, while a track like 'Mausam / Broken Hearted One' layers its melodies till its shapes obscure into a bed. All of these instances give 'AFTERIMAGE' an ambient effect but with a dynamic character, creating a standout lexicon for the album that is truly its crown jewel.

Meanwhile, the influence of the folk canon, no doubt informed by Ahmed's academic and curatorial work on South Asian female folk musical traditions, opens up the themes of the album from just the diaspora experience to anyone who has had to move away from loved ones, said emotional goodbyes, felt the need for them and longed for the life before them at the same time.

The English-language songwriting on the album does add variation to the album, but they don't share the perfect marriage with the placating soft instrumentation and the focused sentimentality of the patient melodic expression on a single word that the Braj, Hindustani and Urdu counterparts feature. It's the latter world where 'AFTERIMAGE' functions best, creating a sonic world where it can take flight into shoegazy crescendos like on 'Mother I Have To Leave' or stay convinced in a memorable, delicate performance as in 'Jaat Rahi'.

Listen to 'Afterimage' below and follow Slowspin for more information.

Image: Slowspin & executive producer, bassist and synth player Shahzad Ismaily by Tonje Thileson

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生的肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo及Olith Ratengo合作完成，是内罗毕厂牌Cool Waters的首张发行。音乐以Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手打击乐和套鼓为驱动，叠加83岁老歌手Nengo所传承的dodo传统唱腔，以及Ratengo与之呼应的嗓音。曲目如《Bara》从重复的机械敲击逐渐引入4/4节拍、低音与类木琴音色，合成器复节奏层层渗透，最终与歌声融为一体；《Sarah》则以人声为主导，边缘失真适时强化紧迫感。专辑在电子声响与肯尼亚传统根源之间建立动态平衡，既保留文化脉络，又让实验元素自然生长，体现了21世纪全球音乐语境下传统与科技的有机对话。

items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利前卫作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino及诗人Luca Chino Ferrari的合作，延续了她自60年代实验乐队以来的先锋精神。音乐以钢琴为核心，通过相位错位、叠加与前景/背景的游移，配合弦乐、木管、合成器与金属质感声响，构建出非线性、调式化的氛围织体，刻意挑战西方传统和声的听觉惯性。歌词兼具诗意与直接的政治锋芒，《Pale Wanderer》触及威权主义所需的共谋，《Charlottesville》影射现实中的种族主义暴力，同时也不乏对死亡与人类在宇宙中位置的沉思。Moskowitz的嗓音以近似方法派演员的权威感嵌入文本，旋律如意识流般起伏，钢琴则充当另一声部乃至希腊歌队式的评论者。整体上，这是一张将前卫作曲、氛围声响与艺术歌曲传统融合的作品，在听觉与思想上均具有持续的挑衅性。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家奥马尔·索萨在疫情隔离与个人生活动荡期间，受邀于意大利法齐奥利钢琴厂音乐厅进行了一场无脚本的两小时即兴独奏，随后在混音中加入稀疏的人声片段、打击乐、循环乐句、田野录音与拾得声音效果，形成这张《Sendas》。作品延续了索萨受蒙克启发的“绝不重复”理念，以第一遍录音为灵魂，强调自然流露与“少即是多”的美学。音乐在钢琴弦内的拨奏与抚触中展开，营造出深邃共鸣，又融入低音喉音式泛音与冥想般的节奏律动，体现艺术家对精神失落时代的回应——扎根传统又坚定前行。专辑跨越爵士、世界音乐与实验声响的边界，拒绝风格归类，以即兴与直觉驱动，呈现出一种兼具沉思性与进化感的独特声音旅程。

items.body: Tapestries brings together works written over more than a decade, yet it never feels like a retrospective. From the opening bars of “Chartres” to the closing “La muë,” the album displays an unmistakable coherence of language even when each composition retains its distinct character. From the architectural “Chartres” to the guttural “Incantare,” from the hallucinatory “Datura” to the metamorphic “La muë,” Justina Repečkaitė‘s music unfolds patiently, asking the listener to focus on the smallest changes in resonance and colour. Its range of references makes this a highly rewarding journey. Medieval stained glass, manuscripts, birdsong, healing charms, poisonous plants and eighteenth-century medical treatises all become starting points for the music. None of these references is treated as programme music or illustration. Instead, Repečkaitė translates them into musical structures that develop according to their own internal logic. The opening “Chartres” immediately establishes this approach. Strings emerge from silence with a cold, almost glacial sonority, creating an acoustic space that expands incrementally. Throughout the album, the ensemble often behaves as a single resonating body rather than a collection of individual instruments. Voices, strings, winds and electronics continually merge, dissolve and reappear, producing a remarkably fluid sound world. One of the album’s most striking works is “Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus.” Inspired by the silence of the pandemic lockdown, Repečkaitė recorded starling calls and plays them back through tiny speakers hidden inside the piano. The electronics become inseparable from the instrument itself, creating the impression that the bird has become trapped within the piano’s resonating body. As the keyboard gradually expands across its register, the birdsong remains dependent on each hammer strike, allowing a simple compositional idea to become a reflection on confinement and the desire to break free. Transformation also lies at the heart of “Datura,” the shortest track on the album. Here the trombonist simultaneously plays, sings and recites botanical descriptions of the poisonous plant whose two principal alkaloids induce either delirium or numbness. Once again, the extended techniques never feel demonstrative. They emerge naturally from the musical idea, allowing the instrument and the voice to occupy the same expressive space. That permeability between voice and instrument runs throughout the album. Singing performers, hybrid timbres and discreet electronics continually broaden the acoustic field. The closing “La muë” brings many of these ideas together. Drawing on an eighteenth-century treatise on the changing adolescent voice, the work combines children’s choir, electronics and the extraordinary sound of the serpent, played and sung simultaneously by Patrick Wibart. Listening to Tapestries, one gradually realises that Repečkaitė is not interested in translating images into music. She is interested in translating systems of thought. Architecture becomes form, birdsong becomes resonance, botanical knowledge becomes gesture, and the changing human voice becomes an evolving sonic landscape. Justina Repečkaitė at Ircam, 2024. Photo Kristijonas Naslenas To expand on the album, Justina Repečkaitė has answered a few questions for us by email. Tapestries spans compositions written between 2012 and 2024 and traces a path from solo works to orchestral and interdisciplinary pieces. Looking back across these twelve years, what threads do you now see connecting these seemingly different works into a single artistic tapestry? I believe that already in “Chartres” (2012) one can recognise the foundations of my musical language, which becomes progressively more complex in “La muë” (2024). My compositions have pre-compositional keys, in the album there is only an exemple of “Chartres”, because its link with the stained glass window is visually speaking. Across the works, different musical parameters are tightly interconnected, often generating a sense of pulsation, cyclical time and organised harmony, governed by arithmetic logic. In purely instrumental pieces such as “Chartres” (2012), “Tapisserie” (2015), and “Vellum” (2020), there are structural affinities in which the ensemble builds a shared architectural form, rather than a collection of individual parts, individualities. This architectural thinking also persists in “La Cité des Dames” (2018) and in the vocal writing of “La Muë”, though there it is articulated through the presence of text – whether as resistance in “La Cité des Dames” or transformation in “La Muë”. Another recurring thread is the permeability between voice and instrument. My instrumental writing is often described as vocal, while my vocal writing is conceived in a similarly instrumental manner. Singing while playing the instruments appears in several works: the trombone in “Datura” (2021), the serpent in “La Muë” (2024), and the flute in “Incantare” (2018). Even “Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus” can be understood as “singing,” since its electronics are derived from a short starling song that resonates with and colours every piano gesture. In the works with electronics, its function is an expansion of the instrument, opening its acoustic space and extending its resonance. More broadly, many of my works reference manuscripts, traditions, or historical practices because they feed my imagination. Architectural and visual forms appear throughout your work, from the stained glass of “Chartres” to the textile references of “Tapisserie” and the manuscript imagery of “Vellum”. What attracts you to these material and architectural metaphors, and how do they influence your compositional thinking? Before I turned to composition, I was preparing to study visual arts, so my artistic education was rooted in images rather than in music. That background has never disappeared. I have a particular fascination with the medieval world, where architecture, manuscripts and textiles reveal systems in which proportion, number and geometry generate beauty. As a composer who often works with rigorous underlying structures, I find it inspiring to see how rules and constraints can produce forms of remarkable richness and expressivity. These references are therefore more than poetic metaphors or title inspirations. They influence how I conceive musical form. I am inspired by the idea that a score might possess an autonomous existence, almost like an architectural drawing, a textile pattern or a draft manuscript: a carefully constructed object whose internal organisation embodies ideas before it is ever brought into sound. I carefully craft the pre-compositional keys of my works, as they gather the essential logic and structure of a piece on a single page, like a blueprint of the musical form. Voice occupies a special place in your music. In “Incantare,” “Datura,” and “La muë,” performers sing while playing their instruments, creating hybrid timbres that blur the boundary between body and instrument. What first drew you to this technique, and what does it allow you to express that conventional instrumental writing cannot? I first experimented with simultaneous singing and playing technique while writing Toro (2015) for electronics and the euphonium player Vianney Desplantes, who taught me a great deal about it. What interests me in this fusion of sounds is the emergence of a hybrid timbre, in which the boundary between body and instrument becomes porous. The voice is the most intimate instrument, and when it is projected through another instrument, it produces a very personal and unstable sound – never identical from one performer to another! As I am also a singer, I do not separate vocal production from instrumental sound; for me they belong to the same continuum of expression. For example, Incantare has been performed by both male and female flutists, across different vocal ranges and instruments, and each interpretation reveals a distinct version of the piece. In this sense, the work exists less as a fixed object than as a living transformation shaped by performers. Several pieces transform non-musical materials into musical structures: Lithuanian healing charms in Incantare, birdsong in “Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus,” Christine de Pizan’s feminist text in “La Cité des Dames,” and an eighteenth-century treatise on puberty in “La muë.” How do you approach the process of translating historical, literary, or natural phenomena into sound? The pieces you mention were written during moments of intense creative momentum. I found the ideas behind them so compelling that the process often felt less like inventing something from nothing and more like uncovering something that was already present. The initial spark of Incantare (2018), La Cité des Dames (2019) , Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus (2020), and La muë (2024) was so strong that my role as a composer was to reveal and shape its musical potential. For me, music is not separate from other cultural or natural forms; rather, it is a space where they can be transformed and reconfigured into sound. I am not interested in illustrating a text, a historical source, or a natural phenomenon, but in identifying the structures, gestures, rhythms, materials, and energies within them that can generate a musical language of their own. This is perhaps why I never use a text in its entirety, but rather extract fragments that contain the essential qualities I want to transform through composition. “La Cité des Dames” draws on Christine de Pizan’s visionary text about creating a symbolic city for women, while “La muë” explores transformation through adolescence, voice, and bodily change. Do questions of identity, gender, and embodiment play a broader role in your work, even when they are not explicitly foregrounded? In these two pieces, identity is primordial. In “La Cité des Dames,” Christine de Pizan’s text describes women creating a symbolic space of their own in a society where their voices were marginalized. The fact that the work is written for six soprano parts makes the female voice itself part of its meaning. In La muë, the subject is the adolescent voice changing during puberty. The voice becomes a marker of bodily transformation and identity. The child singers, the serpent player who sings through the instrument, and the electronics all expand the relationship between body, instrument, and sound. Beyond these two works, I am often interested in states of transition, where change is still unfolding. This is true both conceptually and at the smallest level of my music, where repetition is never static but constantly transformed through timbre, dynamics, and context. In “La Cité des Dames” and “La muë,” the body and voice become central because they are themselves sites of transformation: the collective female voice reclaiming a space of expression in the former, and the changing adolescent voice in the latter. Your music is often described as balancing rigorous construction with organic, almost living sonic processes. One critic compared your compositions to cycles of germination, growth, blossoming, and decay. Do you think of your works primarily as structures to be built, or as organisms that evolve according to their own internal logic? I begin with rigorously constructed structures, and then let the musical material grow organically within them. The structuring process can be demanding, sometimes involving the abandonment of many ideas, but once the framework is in place, the music begins to move freely inside it, as if the architecture itself begins to sing. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: 立陶宛作曲家Justina Repečkaitė的专辑汇集十余年创作，以统一的音乐语言贯穿始终。专辑从建筑性的《Chartres》开场，到变形般的《La muë》收束，作品不依赖标题音乐式的描绘，而是将中世纪彩色玻璃、手稿、鸟鸣、疗愈咒语、有毒植物及十八世纪医学论著等素材转化为遵循内在逻辑展开的音乐结构。乐器与人声不断融合、消散、再现，形成液态般的音响空间。《Sturnus vulgaris cohibitus》录制椋鸟鸣声并通过藏于钢琴内部的小型扬声器回放，电子声响与钢琴本体不可分割，将封锁中的孤独感转化为具体的作曲语言。《Datura》中长号手同时演奏、歌唱并朗诵植物学描述，声音与乐器共享同一表达场域。整张专辑在人声与乐器、传统与电子之间持续拓展声学边界。

items.body: New Zealand artist Abby Helasdottir has been active for many years; she released her debut work twenty-five years ago, and many more have followed since. In recent years, the project has been primarily associated with the Winter-Light label. “Níu Kom Ek Heima Fyr Niflhel Neðan” serves as the final installment of a trilogy that began in 2021 with “Ár Var Alda.” The work revolves around the imagery of nine underworlds, evoking a chthonic reflection of the Norse cosmos akin to Kabbalistic mysticism. Musically, the theme translates into an exquisitely detailed production featuring an impressive sonic canvas. Amidst the myriad sound manipulations, effects, and field recordings, the artist crafts a sophisticated composition that ensnares the listener in an imaginary web. While the atmosphere does not always fully come across—likely due to the sheer scale of the sonic arsenal—one quickly senses the work’s darker side. Although I have known Gydja to experiment less in the past, this remains a remarkable sonic experience from an artist who clearly approaches her work from a unique perspective. The genre sits somewhere between Dark-Ambient, Cinematic, and pure Experimental music. The final track delivers a true apotheosis, blending quiet Tribal elements with a magnificent Eastern atmosphere. If you are looking for a breath of fresh air within established genres like Dark-Ambient and Cinematic music, this work is certainly worth a listen. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Heidthornir”: Heidthornir by Gydja About Gydja Gydja is the dark ambient project of Abby Helasdottir, a musician and graphic artist based in Wellington, New Zealand. The project name is an Old Norse word for priestess, and Helasdottir has described the music as dark ambience for dark goddesses. Alongside her own recordings she has produced cover artwork for a range of releases, including titles issued by Cold Spring. The project dates back to the start of the 2000s, with the CDR “The Darkness Gathering” appearing on Mediatrix in 2001. Later solo work includes “Umbilicus Maris” in 2007 and “Helchemy” in 2009. Helasdottir was one of the artists on the Cryo Chamber collaborative album “Nyarlathotep” in 2016. She also records as Bestia Astrum. More recent releases have come through the Dutch label Winter-Light, which issued the trilogy completed by this album. It opened with “Ár Var Alda” in 2021, built around the primordial void Ginnungagap, and continued with “Þjóðáar Fnæstu Eitri”, which took the eleven-fold river Élivágar as its subject. The closing title is drawn from the Old Norse poem “Vafþrúðnismál”. “Níu Kom Ek Heima Fyr Niflhel Neðan” was released on 8 May 2026 on digital and CD. Helasdottir recorded and produced the album at Ultrasound between 2024 and 2025, handled the graphic design, and Robin Storey mastered it.

items._cn_summary: Gydja（Abby Helasdottir）以三部曲终章呈现这张专辑，主题围绕北欧神话中九个冥界的意象展开，音乐上对应为丰富的声学编织。作品运用大量声音操控、效果处理与田野录音，营造出精巧复杂的声场结构，将听众引入一张想象的网中。终曲融合了安静的部落元素与东方气息，形成整张专辑的高潮段落。作为一位活跃二十五年的新西兰艺术家，她以独到的视角进行创作，作品横跨暗氛围、电影配乐与纯实验音乐之间。该专辑在2024至2025年间录制完成，由Robin Storey负责母带处理，在独立厂牌Winter-Light发行。

items.body:
On her third studio album, Brooklyn-based artist Frances Chang feels out the boundary between bedroom pop and lavishly orchestrated avant-experimentation, writing on a century-old grand piano and spiking her productions with jerky, unconventional electronic elements. The end result is somewhere between Aimee Mann and Cate Le Bon.

There's something unmistakably ramshackle about Chang's productions, but at the same time, it all sounds as if it's been meticulously planned. On opening track 'I can feel the waves', her voice never falters as it soars over casual phrases from her aging baby grand, but the it's the beats that immediately catch your attention, rupturing the calm with the momentum of a footwork demo. Chang's clearly an obsessive listener and it's this passion that lends her songs a breath of originality; they're classic in a sense, informed by Burt Bacharach, Chet Baker and Dionne Warwick, which actually makes sense. And where she takes the songs after they've been written is fascinating, building them out with instrumentation that's not exactly unexpected, it's just ever so slightly off-kilter. Those warbling strings on the ace 'Bad zen', or the buzzing micro-repetitions on 'Marry' - these sounds just nudge the material into a different zone and assert Chang's personality.

And as it develops, Chang's confidence grows. She's most successful when the guardrails are fully off - like on the brilliant 'No avatar'. Here, she latches her Robert Ashley-esque vocal lead to a wonky synth arpeggio that she follows with piano - or vice versa? The other instruments coolly fall into line: drums, bass and organ seem to flutter, flourish and fall at Chang's command, never quite going in the expected direction. Even advance single 'Auratones of Desire' makes more sense in context, its well-sculpted fusion of psych drum breaks, frittered farfisa organs and soft vocal affectations widening the album's reach considerably. Given it some time and attention for full reward.
items._cn_summary: Frances Chang在第三张专辑中探索卧室流行与先锋实验的边界，以百年老钢琴为创作基底，融入不规则的电子声响。人声在松散钢琴短语上平稳游走，节拍却以脚踩舞曲般的动量打破平静。歌曲结构受Burt Bacharach、Chet Baker等经典影响，但配器处理偏离常规，如弦乐颤音与微重复音色。后半张更放开限制，人声与合成器琶音交错，鼓、贝斯、管风琴等乐器随其指令流动。整体在精心编排与即兴感之间取得平衡，需要时间细听才能充分领会。

items.body:
Barnt’s mnml 2012 kosmische waltzer for Matias Aguayo’s Cómeme is repackaged with a new master and Jens-Uwe Beyer + Crato revisions.

The kinky schaeffel is in effect on ‘gaffe’, which takes on a 2nd wind in its brighter, robust remaster, while Jens Uwe-Beyer evens out its irregularities for a disco-ready remix, and best of all, a ‘Magazine Hallucination’ mix that initially jettisons the beat and opens upwards, outward into majestic ambient zones, before its pulled back in a screwed echo of the original waltz groove.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Barnt于2012年为Cómeme厂牌发行的作品，此次以重新母带版本面世，并附有Jens-Uwe Beyer与Crato的混音。原曲在更明亮饱满的remaster中焕发新的活力，Beyer的混音则抚平了原曲的不规则律动，使其更贴近舞池。最突出的是‘Magazine Hallucination’混音，它先剥离节拍，向上向外敞开，进入宏大的氛围地带，随后又被拉回原版华尔兹律动的扭曲回响中。整体在极简律动与宇宙感氛围之间游走，兼具实验性与可舞性，适合喜欢氛围电子与kosmische风格的听众。

items.body:
The spirit of legendary film score composer Toru Takemitsu looms large over Kotaro Maruyama’s economical yet lush studies, ranging from sublime echoes of Japanese environmental ambient to beatific pulse poems edging on weightless Heinrich Mueller works.

"Composing primarily with the piano, Kotaro Maruyama creates music for a variety of visual media, including commercials and short films. Influenced by the composer Toru Takemitsu, he places importance on the “silence” and "ambience" of sound, aiming to create works where the music quietly depicts a scene.

Kotaro Maruyama's first solo album, "Vapor Curve," is constructed entirely from the sound source of the OP-Z digital synthesizer. Notably, he avoids the concept of harmony for a single tone, instead pursuing a unique "woven harmony" created by intricately layering multiple independent melodies. Using only the OP-Z, and recording everything in a single take without using a computer, Kotaro Maruyama's "Vapor Curve" is distinguished by its uncompromising production style. The minimalist melodies that are layered to create an ambient soundscape, along with the incidental noise that gives an organic texture to the inorganic electronic sound, showcase the raw appeal of sound that is imperfect."
items._cn_summary: 丸山浩太郎的首张个人专辑以一台数字合成器为唯一音源，并采用一次录音完成、不借助电脑的创作方式。他刻意回避单一音色的和声概念，转而通过多条独立旋律的精密叠加，形成所谓“编织和声”。在武满彻式对静默与氛围的重视下，极简旋律铺展出近似日本环境音乐的声响景观，而偶然噪声为无机电子音色注入有机质感。整张专辑在限制中探索声音的不完美与现场感，其制作路径明显偏离电子音乐惯常的工作流程。

items.body:
Influential Brum punks/post-punks Swell Maps captured in their snotty pomp, 1979, for the legendary John Peel Sessions - just a year before disbanding, and prompting everyone from Sonic Youth to Nirvana in their wake.

“Noisy, chaotic, and defiantly experimental, Swell Maps may not have found commercial success in their time, but their impact on music is undeniable. An inspiration to bands such as R.E.M., Sonic Youth, Dinosaur Jr., Pavement and Nirvana, with Kurt Cobain famously being a fan and often seen sporting a Swell Maps T-Shirt. A democracy within the confines of punk’s anything is possible, members Biggles Books, Jowe Head and brothers Nikki Sudden and Epic Soundtracks—helped shape the landscape of post-punk and DIY music. Now, for the first time in over 40 years, The John Peel Sessions brings together all three of their recordings for John Peel, a figure instrumental in championing their sound.

Formed in the early ’70s and fully realised by 1976, Swell Maps embodied the DIY ethos, launching their own label and self-releasing the jagged, frenetic debut single ‘Read About Seymour’ in 1978. Peel was an early supporter, playing their record as soon as it landed on his desk—a moment the band described as one of disbelief and elation. His regular airplay of their music helped solidify their cult status, and these sessions capture the raw energy, off-kilter melodies, and boundary-pushing creativity that defined them."
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了Swell Maps于1979年为John Peel节目录制的三场现场录音，乐队在次年解散，这些作品定格了他们短暂而高产的创作巅峰。Swell Maps以DIY精神为核心，自创厂牌并自行发行首支单曲，音乐上融合了朋克的粗粝噪音与后朋克的实验倾向，旋律偏离常规，结构松散而充满即兴冲动。John Peel的持续播放为他们奠定了地下 cult 地位，这些录音保留了乐队最原始的能量和即兴碰撞的现场感。作为影响过Sonic Youth、Nirvana、Pavement等乐队的源头之一，Swell Maps在历史语境中的价值通过这次再版得以清晰呈现，也让人重新审视那些未被商业体系收编的独立声音如何塑造了后朋克与独立音乐的版图。

items.body:
Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.
items._genre: deep techno / dub techno / ambient / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张EP是Sa Pa在自创厂牌Dub Techno For Life的首发作品，四首曲目在俱乐部律动与实验声响之间展开。A面以十分钟的厚重滚动节拍向Andreas Tilliander致敬，同时保留Teutonic house的极简优雅；B面则转向更粗粝的质感，融合了苦涩泥泞的低频推进与类似Actress或Rezzett式的抽象回旋。整体上既呈现了艺术家最扎实的舞曲面向，也容纳了ambient与声音设计的实验倾向，被视为一张展现其创作光谱的自画像式发行。

items.body:
Club Romantico salute an unsung pioneer of modern club movements, Daniel Pineda ov Nguzunguzu - a producer of early Kelela and the short-lived Future Brown with Fatima Al-Qadiri - with a handful of lush yet venomous originals plus a Kelman Duran link-up 

You can’t talk about the 2010’s club sound without acknowledging Daniel Pineda’s influential, border-smudging productions as half of Nguzunguzu, with Asthma Maroof. Along with the likes of Total Freedom, Pineda’s work ushered the freshest wave of syncopated club music from the US at a time when Night Slugs (and Numbers.) and its American division, Fade To Mind, were hybridising UKF with Latin house, Jersey and B-More club and a groundswell of virulent Global South rhythms that began to percolate Westwards via blogs (this was the salient stuff when talking about blog-era, not the fidget-house pish) by the end of the ‘00s. 

Pineda’s ‘Landlocked’ firmly marks his return to a scene he sowed nearly decades ago, swerving from the heart-in-mouth pads and Dutch Bubblers-type groove to ‘De La Mama’, a a slower variant of that tresillo formula in ‘Gritos’, via the full-bore 145BPM intensity of ‘Fuerte’, a video clash-meets-Ballroom romp ‘Heavy Fact’, and the pneumatic subs and drill clack of a ‘Quema’ primed for carnival season. Another crucial bridge of Global South and Western club music, Kelman Duran tags in on the EP’s slowest, heaviest, ‘Loko 4 Eva’, strapped with below-belt quake and hardest drum cadence bound to get crowds slapping the walls.
items._genre: experimental club / global bass / deconstructed club / electronic
items._cn_summary: 《内陆》是丹尼尔·皮内达（恩古祖恩古祖成员、早期凯莱拉与未来布朗制作人）在罗曼蒂科俱乐部厂牌发行的唱片，标志其回归舞曲场景。作品在丰润与狠辣之间游走：从减速的三连音节奏、每分钟145拍的高强度段落，到融合舞厅文化与钻头节拍的律动，呈现跨地域的俱乐部声响。与凯尔曼·杜兰合作的曲目是唱片中最慢最重的一首，以低频震动和密集鼓组制造压迫感。皮内达延续了十年前以恩古祖恩古祖推动的边界模糊制作思路，将拉丁浩室、泽西与巴尔的摩俱乐部等美国地下传统同当代钻头和舞厅语言重新焊接，体现其对全球南方俱乐部音乐脉络的独特连接。

items.body:
More slick sophisti-pop from the CPH scene, Gustav Berntsen's follow-up to 2024's Posh Isolation-released 'Gusse Music' is inspired by Japanoise and jazz fusion and rooted in collaged Metro stories - go figure.

Berntsen was stationed in London when he was writing 'Herzprung' and began to collect copies of the infamous free rag Metro, that he cut to shreds to fix up the lyrical portion of the songs. Once he had this in check, the Danish singer-songwriter called up his most trusted collaborators and booked a week at a studio "in the Swedish wilderness", where he dubbed the songs live to 24-track tape, encouraging improvisation and collaboration. And there's certainly a knottiness to this material that's unique to Bernsten; like many contemporary Copenhagen-based operatives, he's clearly well versed in classic rock and pop, from Fleetwood Mac and Steely Dan to Chick Corea and Haruomi Hosono, but he doesn't stop at pastiche, instead bringing his own absurdities to the table (via Metro). "The Simpson's Season Six," he calls out harmoniously on opener 'Adrenaline', interrupting a stop-start drum fill and riffs that wouldn't sound out of place on a Gastr del Sol record. 

It would be hard to label 'Herzprung' post-rock, but there's a sense that Berntsen has at least learned from the genre's Chicago-era excesses. He seems to be driven by a holistic understanding of pop; at their heart, his songs are impeccably written, yet he's also not interested in taking the clearest path. On 'Belly', his cool-headed harmonies and almost tropicalia-strength choruses are complicated by winding instrumental sections and a phenomenally atmospheric dip into tape-fuckt cosmic ambience, while the lengthy 'Shit River' is a slowcore anthem that Berntsen expands with a full choir and an arsenal of synths.
items._genre: sophisti-pop / experimental / jazz fusion / art pop
items._cn_summary: 丹麦音乐人Gustav Berntsen在专辑中延续了哥本哈根场景的精致流行路线，却以Japanoise与爵士融合为灵感，将Metro免费报纸剪碎拼贴成歌词，并在瑞典荒野的录音室中以24轨磁带现场即兴录制。作品在经典摇滚与流行基底上注入实验性编排，如《Adrenaline》中打断式的鼓组与《辛普森一家》第六季的念白，或《Belly》里蜿蜒的器乐段落与磁带失真环境氛围，以及《Shit River》以合唱和合成器扩展的慢核长曲。整体既保有扎实的歌曲写作，又拒绝直线路径，呈现出一种糅合流行触感与实验冲动的独特质感。

items.body:
Tighter and tidier than last year's 'Electric Chair', Cities Aviv's latest set is a psilocybin-infused dream sequence packed with fuzzy ambient interludes, loopy clouded reflections and stream-of-consciousness recitations. 

 Gavin Mays has always been on the perimeter of any given scene or other, happy enough to draw his own landscape while everyone else churns up the same mud. And that's truer than ever on his recent run; operating on his lonesome, Mays creates music that can't be pigeonholed - it's barely even rap. He spits on the two-part title track, but his words dilate awkwardly over noisy, new age-esque synths and blown-out, pitch-deformed rhythms. They might not even be strictly on the beat at all, that's not the point - Mays creates a mood that he prolongs throughout 'Even Colder Spring'. The second part of the title track sounds more like Seefeel than it does MF DOOM, anyways.

It's not always easy to digest - we'll admit we struggled with 'Spinnin & Spinnin' - but 'Even Colder Spring' is surprisingly approachable compared with many of his recent releases. And what it lacks in cohesion it more than makes up for in pure eccentricity. "Maybe Mars is bougie," he quips over electric piano arpeggios and feedback squeals on 'Tribeca', before breathing lullabies over slowed-down soul samples on 'Concrete Masks'.
items._genre: experimental hip hop / ambient / electronic / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了Cities Aviv一贯的游离姿态，在说唱基底上注入大量迷幻氛围段落、模糊的循环反射与意识流念白。人声时常脱离节拍，与失真的音高变形节奏、噪音化合成器交织，形成介于说唱与氛围电子之间的暧昧地带。部分曲目更偏向早期Seefeel式的声响纹理，而非传统说唱逻辑。整体听感松散却充满怪诞趣味，如Tribeca中电钢琴琶音与反馈尖鸣之上的即兴调侃，或Concrete Masks中放缓灵魂采样后的摇篮曲气息。专辑并不追求连贯性，而是以纯粹的 eccentricity 取胜，在嘈杂与柔和的落差中构建出独特的情绪场域。对于偏好实验声响与跨界融合的听者而言，这是一次值得深入的声音漫游。

items.album: Around Here, The Birds Plant The Trees
items.excerpt: Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees. ‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with
items.body:
Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees.

‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with a local farmer on how “birds are the architects of the living landscape”. It follows some 40 solo albums over the past 20 years (not to mention jams with Woven Skull and Tomuttontu) with a considered approach to what lies just beyond her home; typically drawing on her attentive reading of the rural soundsphere to transmute the poetry of birdsong and the natural world into expressive musical metaphor.

The low bowed cello tone of regular spar Eimear Reidy underlines and opens out a breezy space where where the fiddle and violinists criss-cross air in reserved melodic flight and plucky figures that alternate like the play of light on Ireland’s remote North West. The piece unfolds to boggy pockets of percussion and passages of barely-there, hushed gloam, as though the wind itself was generating the players’ gestures, which rise to cloud castle hover around the midway, only to depart for Nyahh label boss Willie Stewart’s rolling drum thunder and scrape of Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh's fiddle rooted in the rolling landscape. Ultimately the folk soul of the turf rises in its final section, resembling a rousing, swaying folk song voiced by the strings in ideally creaky discord.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Natalia Beylis为五重奏创作的长篇环境音乐作品，灵感源自黑鸟晨鸣以及当地农民关于鸟类是景观建筑师的说法。大提琴的低沉音色铺展出开阔空间，小提琴与提琴的旋律线条交错，如同爱尔兰西北部光影的流动。打击乐与近乎无声的段落形成沼泽般的节奏凹陷，仿佛风本身在驱动演奏者的动作。中段之后转向滚动的鼓声与提琴刮擦，最终以带有民间灵魂的摇摆曲调收束。值得聆听之处在于，Beylis将鸟鸣诗学与乡村声景的细致观察转化为音乐隐喻，以缓慢展开的织体呈现自然逻辑，在环境音乐与民谣根源之间建立了独特的表达。

items.body:
A quiet show of strength from Chicago’s budding and already highly sought after Dub Techno specialists, Kino Disk, hustling 11 exclusive permutations of dub-suffixed ambient, techno, and elemental abstraction by label regulars and new figures including Eustress, Infant, 8004 and many others, huge tip FFO Chain Reaction, Huerco S., Echospace, Short Span, Vialan.

In the space of 20 odd releases since 2024, Kino Disk has emerged as a key point of interest for off-grid dub aficionados. ‘American Dub Electronics’ now opens an ideal entry portal to their microcosm, rendering 11 exclusive bits that speak to the label’s fine grasp of variation within a theme. Trust it’s not wall-to-wall mark & moritz worship, rather a webbed spectra of interrelated, American POV’s on the same gauzy spirit from their collected vapours.

Building on the smouldering embers of over 30 years of precedents in this field, the set sways from the moonlit tidal movement of Psalm Star Electric’s ‘001’ to the unmoored slosh of 8006 (whose ‘8004’ was a sleeper gem of ’25) with a particularly nocturnal appeal. Eustress practices the most Catholic form of dub house in the darkly luminous ‘mm’, and Eden Aurelius’ Ring impress with the ASMR-like sensitivities of ‘Changeling’, and another label regular Point Survey with the phasing dub noise of ‘Print-Through’.

Keener observers may recognise those names already, but perhaps not the new ones here, notably Corbin Cary & Taylor White’s Permutia duo, secreting the fine lather chords and sandman bassline of ‘p1.2’, or HPIN with the early SND-style puckered glitch of ‘Remote’, Uos’ washed-out textures on Uos in ‘Uos Jelly’, and dreamily poised dub waltz of ‘Speedwalker’ by a.m.p & b.p.p.
items._genre: dub techno / ambient / electronic / glitch / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Kino Disk厂牌旗下11首独家曲目，围绕dub式氛围、techno与抽象声响展开。作品并非对经典dub techno的简单模仿，而是在同一主题下呈现多种变体：从月光般潮汐流动的ambient，到失重摇摆的dub律动，再到带有ASMR质感的细节处理和类似早期SND的微声glitch。参与音乐人包括Eustress、Infant、8004、Point Survey等，既有厂牌常客也有新面孔，整体呈现出美国地下电子场景对dub遗产的独特视角，声音层次细腻，适合关注实验电子与氛围舞曲的听众。

An evergreen.. "Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold
items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是约翰·柯川在《A Love Supreme》之后继续向精神自由爵士推进的重要作品，录制于1966年。经典四重奏（麦考伊·泰纳、吉米·加里森、埃尔文·琼斯）最后一次完整集结，并加入费罗·桑德斯与拉希德·阿里，形成更庞大的打击乐与萨克斯编制。音乐在高度抽象的能量即兴与相对克制的优美段落之间切换，放弃传统曲式，转向对声响本身和精神性的追问。专辑既延续了柯川对自由爵士的探索，也记录了他晚期音乐语言中强度与奉献并存的转变，是其录音遗产中具有转型意义的文献。

items.body:
Josephine Foster and The Victor Herrero Band release "Anda Jaleo / Pearlas" via Fire Records.

"Anda Jaleo was originally released in 2010. Federico Garcia Lorca's popular folk song collection "Las Canciones Populares Espanolas" was banned under Franco's dictatorship and today the music survives but marginally within the Spanish sub-conscious. Taking their cue from Lorca and La Argentinita's infectious 1931 recording of the songs, Josephine Foster and her partner Spanish musician Victor Herrero arranged the poetically rich collection for their acoustic band, formed while living in the Grenadine Sierra. Anda Jaleo is the band's live recording of "Las Canciones"; a visceral celebration of the persistence of popular anonymous song. This new edition includes an additional track not featured on the original release, an interpretation of ‘Sones de Asturias’. La colección de "Canciones Populares Españolas" recopiladas y armonizadas por Federico García Lorca fue censurada en tiempos de Franco, y hoy en día la música sobrevive aunque de una manera vaga en el subconsciente del pueblo español. Inspirados por la contagiosa grabación de las canciones de Lorca y La Argentinita de 1931, Josephine Foster y su compañero el músico español Víctor Herrero han arreglado esta poética y rica colección para su banda acústica , formada mientras vivían en la sierra de Granada. Anda Jaleo es la grabación en directo de su versión de "Las Canciones"; una celebración visceral de la canción popular anónima y su persistencia. Following from Anda Jaleo, Josephine Foster and the Victor Herrero Band created a superb follow-up entitled Perlas (Pearls). It is a jewel of a collection, with songs and poems selected by Josephine herself, gathered from dusty old scores and brought vividly to the present with warm performances full of flesh-and-blood emotion. Made with a variety of stringed instruments and simple percussion, the songs were recorded live in the studio on to analogue tape by Paco Loco in Puerto de Santa Maria, Spain. Foster breathes new life into timeless traditional melodies, drawing from the Spanish-folk traditions of Castile, the Basque, Santander and the Costa Brava."
items._genre: spanish folk / world music / acoustic / traditional
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了约瑟芬·福斯特与维克托·埃雷罗乐队的两张作品。《Anda Jaleo》源于洛尔卡与拉·阿亨蒂尼塔1931年录音的启发，将洛尔卡收集的西班牙民歌改编为原声乐队编制，并以现场录音呈现这些曾被弗朗哥政权禁绝的歌曲；新版还追加了《Sones de Asturias》。《Perlas》由福斯特亲自从旧乐谱中挑选歌曲与诗篇，在圣玛丽亚港由帕科·洛科以模拟磁带录制，使用多种弦乐器和简单打击乐，赋予传统旋律以鲜活的血肉感。整体是对西班牙民间音乐传统的当代演绎，兼具文献整理的选曲眼光与亲密的室内乐质感。

items.body:
Beirut-based sound artist and veteran improviser Jad Atoui captures his country's current instability on his latest full-length, performing live in situ with his modular rig.

Ostensibly a noise record, it's inspired by Atoui's early club experiences, where he twigged the physicality of sound for the first time. Here, he uses the same properties to provoke very different responses, layering distorted waves of sound on 'Pressure Dream' that might as well be collapsing buildings. And by recording the material live, there's a distinct human touch that's often missing from this kind of material. Atoui is able to work instinctively, reacting to the sound in the room on the outstanding 'Reaching Heart' as glassy drones bend to corroded rhythmic interjections. 

There's even a glimmer of hope; the gorgeous 'Blue Moon Red Cloud' is a break from stuttering beats and searing noise that hits like an oasis in the desert, lifted by Atoui's freeform melodies and delirious FM chimes.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以模块化合成器在黎巴嫩当地现场录制，直接捕捉国家动荡时期的即兴声响。开篇的扭曲声浪与压迫性噪音并非单纯宣泄，而是延续了艺术家早年俱乐部经历中对声音物理性的感知，让听者感受到空间与情绪的共振。在《Reaching Heart》中，玻璃质感的持续音与腐蚀性节奏穿插，体现出演奏者对现场声场的敏锐反应；而《Blue Moon Red Cloud》则用自由旋律和迷幻FM铃声制造出短暂的宁静，仿佛沙漠中的绿洲。整体上，专辑在噪音与旋律之间保持张力，既有实验性的声音设计，又带有鲜明的地域语境与人性温度，适合偏好前卫声响与即兴表达的听众。

items.body:
Limited edition, first time 2LP re-issue of a compilation originally released via Gary Mundy's legendary Broken Flag imprint in 1987 and featuring a veritable who’s who of post industrial drone and psyche/power electronics including Ramleh, Total, Andrew Chalk and many more.​

"Remastered by Puppy38, this features two bonus tracks not included on the original (and long o/p) LP but only previously found on the even rarer cassette and the equally o/p CD. A timely reminder of this fantastic archive document full of boundary-pushing artists mostly still active in one form or another. Packaged in a sleeve faithful to the distinctive original Cranioclast-designed cover."
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑最初于1987年由Gary Mundy的传奇厂牌Broken Flag发行，集结了Ramleh、Total、Andrew Chalk等后工业噪音与氛围音乐领域的重要人物。此次再版以双LP形式推出，由Puppy38重新母带，并额外收录两首此前仅出现在更稀有磁带版和CD版中的曲目。作品整体呈现出粗粝而富有压迫感的声响景观，融合了长音 drone、电力电子式的失真脉冲以及实验性的音色拼贴，展现了八十年代英国地下音乐场景中极具先锋意识的创作面貌。封面沿用Cranioclast设计的原始视觉，包装忠实还原历史版本。对于关注工业、噪音及实验声响脉络的听众而言，这份档案文献提供了难得的聆听入口。

items.body:
Oh man this is almost too much - just wall to wall genius in action courtesy of Floating Points & Eliot Bernard's Melodies International label -  spotlightling fire in the crown of Mad Professor’s pivotal London Lovers Rock and dub stable, Ariwa Sounds: from an immense monk-steppa ‘Non Violence Dub’ ft. Horace Andy, thru the Motown soul-infused Lovers of Davina Stone on 'Silly Wasn’t I’, to a Kofi gem recently found on Moin’s street-soul/digidub mix, the ruffneck charge of Mafia & Fluxy ‘6 Million Dub’, early Wild Bunch styles on Aisha’s ‘Can You Feel It’, and deadly ‘Liberated Woman’ voiced by Ranking Ann. All killer no filler!

“In 1979, Neil Fraser (artistically known as Mad Professor) founded Ariwa Sounds, the longest-serving and one of the most influential independently owned Reggae studios and record labels in the UK. From humble beginnings set up in the front room of Neil's home in South London recording on 4-track and homemade equipment, Ariwa would go on to record and release over 300 albums including works from some of the most impactful and storied artists of their time in the genres of Reggae, Dub, and Lovers Rock

Whilst our previous release in collaboration with Ariwa captured the label's early sound, a shared performance with Neil in Osaka and regular visits to his South London studio inspired us to assemble this 15-track compilation, showcasing the label's output across 45 years. Our release emphasizes some of the label's greatest vocalists: Johnny Clarke, Sandra Cross, Kofi, U Roy, Sister Nancy, Queen Omega, Aisha, Garnett Cross, Abel Miller, Horace Andy and more — presenting the Motown and Stax influences in the Lovers Rock, but also provides a glimpse into the dubbier and more experimental side of the label, showcasing Ariwa's commitment to quality but also their personality, philosophy and their humour. Love songs, break-up songs, socially engaged songs, dub experimentations — this compilation is not a "best of" Ariwa but a diverse and honest celebration of the label through the lens of Melodies International.”
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑由梅洛迪斯国际厂牌策划，聚焦疯狂教授主理的阿里瓦之声厂牌四十五年间出品的十五首作品。选曲不以“最佳精选”为框架，而是呈现厂牌的多元面向：从霍勒斯·安迪的开场曲到达维娜·斯通受摩城影响的灵魂情歌，再到艾莎、兰金·安等人的声乐作品，兼顾情歌、分手歌、社会议题与声音实验。编选视角强调阿里瓦之声在录音室处理上的个性与幽默，也展现其与灵魂乐、街头放克和数字节拍的交汇。作为独立厂牌长期运作的见证，合辑在历史梳理与聆听体验之间取得平衡，适合关注声音实验、世界音乐与厂牌文化脉络的听众。

items.body:
At the age of 72, "Evil" Graham Lee, the legendary pedal steel pioneer and veteran of the iconic Australian band The Triffids, delivers his first ever album under his own name titled ‘I Think I’m Alone Now’ -  all hazy widescreen lushness iridescent with a timeless intimacy FFO Eno & Lanois, BJ Nilsen, The Necks.

Chiming beautifully with Isle of Jura’s microcosm of far-flung, nostalgic gems, ‘I Think I'm Alone Now’ is arguably the Aussie label’s lushest releases, and one of its few made this century. It serves to tie off an elliptical, 40 year route from “Evil” Graham Lee’s role as part of backing band for Bill Drummond’s solo debut, thru the shivers of his pedal steel guitar that are practically etched on the popular consciousness, thanks to his turn on ‘Madgrugada Eternal’, off The KLF’s landmark 1990 album, ‘Chill Out’ (retitled From Baltimore to Fair Play)’. 

However, Lee plays to a much broader emotional and tonal register across ‘I Think I'm Alone Now’, swanning from calm country vignettes to quietly quizzical, melancholic soloing and fancifully floating harmonic structures, to a standout, titular 15 min panorama that can perhaps be heard to dwell on a lost future promised by the early ‘90s. Here, halcyon days feel just of reach, in the rearview, but Lee still evokes the warmth of their glowing embers with a bloozy soul felt in his tactful, lyrically extended melody and grasp of lustrous overtones, before tilting into the heady swirl of closing question, ‘Is There any Pedal Steel in Heaven?’.
items._cn_summary: 72岁的传奇踏板钢棒吉他手Evil Graham Lee首次以个人名义发表专辑，回顾其从The Triffids到参与KLF《Chill Out》的漫长音乐路径。乐评描述这是一张充满朦胧宽银幕质感的作品，在宁静的乡村小品、忧郁的独奏与漂浮的和声结构之间游走，标题曲长达15分钟，仿佛凝视上世纪90年代初失落未来的余温。专辑被比作Brian Eno、Daniel Lanois、BJ Nilsen与The Necks的交汇，既保留pedal steel的温暖泛音，又融入氛围与实验性的延展，最终以一曲《Is There any Pedal Steel in Heaven?》收束，在怀旧与追问之间形成独特的情绪张力。

items.body: I’ve seen the most magical of all magical rhythm sections in free jazz / improvised music - John Edwards on double bass and Mark Sanders on drums - several times now, the first time as the Foils Quartet with Frank Paul Schubert on saxophone and Matthias Müller on trombone. I was immediately blown away; my jaw literally kept dropping at the musical fireworks the two of them set off. Later, I saw them with Trevor Watts and Veryan Weston, then with Swiss saxophonist Omri Ziegele, and finally, three years ago, with John Butcher. However, the most spectacular gig was a concert with Roscoe Mitchell at the Météo Festival in Mulhouse in 2016. After ten minutes, the audience jumped to their feet and gave a standing ovation, yelling, shouting in pure ecstasy - right in the middle of the piece. Sometimes I think that even a way below-average amateur guitarist like me could play with them, and the result would be - let’s say - not a complete disaster. Because It Happens is part of a gig at Café Oto (the other part, Not So Late , is available on a separate CD), and for this recording, the rhythm twins have enlisted the help of first class Polish saxophonist and bass clarinetist Mikołaj Trzaska. It’s no surprise that the trio is in full swing from the very first seconds,. Sanders stays firmly on the drums, which lends the improvisation a dark, driving character. Trzaska uses this for insanely fast runs, which are nonetheless underpinned by a deep spirituality. Many influences converge in his playing: Coltrane, Brötzmann, Shepp, Parker, and many more. His style is both energetic and subtle, he uses vibrato when appropriate but he can also sound very dry and abstract. Added to this is his excellent timing that leaves plenty of space for Edwards and Sanders. All of this is evident right from the opener “Running Loose”. Throughout the entire set a wide range of emotions is explored; there are moments of intense density followed by very lyrical passages (e.g., in “Creator of Creatures”) and superbly integrated solos (see Sanders’s drum solo in “Written By”). However, the highlight of the album is the encore, “Light Inches”, which Edwards and Sanders kick off with an off-the-wall rhythm. The piece swings back and forth, Trzaska lets the notes dart through the room, breaks off abruptly, plays somewhere in the background, then Edwards takes the lead - the three musicians seem to be arguing over the direction of the improvisation, only to then agree almost instinctively on where to go. The rest is sheer madness in terms of power, harmony, and perfection. Because It Happens is an outstanding album in every respect. Anyone who wants to hear state-of-the-art European free jazz (or “live composition”, as the musicians call it) should give this release a try. Because It Happens is available on vinyl and as a download. Because It Happens by Mikołaj Trzaska, John Edwards, Mark Sanders Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张现场录音由波兰萨克斯手Mikołaj Trzaska与英国节奏组合John Edwards和Mark Sanders合作完成，录制于Café Oto。乐评指出Edwards与Sanders是自由爵士领域极具默契的节奏双人组，Trzaska的演奏融合了Coltrane、Brötzmann等多重影响，兼具爆发力与细腻控制。专辑从开场曲便进入高能状态，在密集即兴与抒情段落之间切换，并包含Sanders的独立鼓独奏。压轴加演曲“Light Inches”中，三人以偏离常规的节奏开场，乐句在萨克斯、贝斯与鼓之间来回碰撞，仿佛在争论即兴方向后又本能地达成一致。整张唱片展现了欧洲自由爵士中“活作曲”的即兴逻辑，属于该领域具有代表性的现场记录。
