items.body: Our cores may have rotted into compost over the summer, but we’ve been churned into the earth and emerged with a collection of releases to share that have given us life this year. I tasked a few of our writers with narrowing down a top 10 for 2026 within a specific sub-genre I knew they’re into, highlighting specifically their number 1 thus far with a brief write-up. Through this we have a hefty list of  forty LPs/EPs, highlighting the best of metalcore/mathcore, screamo/post-hardcore, grindcore, and noise rock that this year has served up so far. So, let’s get to it, and we hope you find some new filth to bask in. -TBPK Shares Their Top 10 Metalcore/Mathcore Releases So Far This YearConverge - Hum of Hurt / Love Is Not Enough I've put the Converge surprise double release of Hum of Hurt and Love Is Not Enough together on this list at number 1...but really that is a bit of a cheat on my part. Hum of Hurt is by far the more emotive, ambitious offering of the two, sitting nicely alongside previous full lengths The Dusk In Us and All We Love We Leave Behind. Standout tracks such as "Detonator" and "Doom in Bloom" are Converge at their brooding, progressive best (and I love that we get to hear Nate's vocals, as a new Doomriders record looks unlikely any time soon). Don't get me wrong, Love Is Not Enough has some killer moments (the title track and "Bad Faith" being two he of them), and it's immensely enjoyable, but overall feels like a slightly one dimensional version of Converge instead of the more complex and multilayered band they've matured into over the last fifteen years. All that being said, we got TWO new Converge albums this year and that makes me very happy indeed.  Hum of Hurt by Converge Chamber - this is goodbye Merit - Sweetness Fades Crowquill - Erase The FilesKicked in the Head by a Horse - BLOOM/DECAY .Gif From God - Dissimulation A Knife in the Dark - Songs Without WitnessThe Absolute Worst or The Absolute Worst - calculusZao - Pillars Temple Guard - Citadel In Flames Crouch - Breaking the Catatonic State This album ended up falling between the cracks on our ‘Best so far’ coverage as it didn't fit into any of our designated genres (we might need to add a ‘Sludge’ list for 2027). It would've been sacrilege to leave it out completely, especially as it's one of my favourite releases of the year so far.It has been well documented that Crouch features members of Oathbreaker and Wiegedood, but it's clear that one of the main influences pulsing through Breaking the Catatonic State is the criminally underrated Knut. Oh how I love Knut. 2002's Challenger is damn near a perfect album in my eyes. This Belgian trio clearly also worship at the altar of the Swiss sludgecore titans, as they effortlessly mix filthy downtuned riffage with slick technicality and clever use of samples. You'll hear some other tips of the cap from 2000's hardcore royalty, such as Coalesce, Converge and Botch in here too. All of these influences have something in common; a resolute anger. That is what fuels everything on this debut full length and the band finds new ways to implement their venom across its ten chapters. I implore you to listen to the whole album from start to finish, but there are a few tracks that stand out. “Vidal” showcases just how musically tight these guys are with a series of complex staccato compositions. “Twisted Colossus” is an absolute monster and does exactly what it says on the tin, but then throws in a wonderful detour that takes the track into unexpected jazz territory. The longest and slowest track on the record crushes everything in its path, and no, I don't think it's a coincidence that this track is titled “Geneva”. The Knut worship may have had me hooked from the start, but the sheer quality of this debut album is difficult to dispute, even for those who don't normally like sludgy hardcore. Without a doubt one of the highlights of 2026 so far.  Breaking The Catatonic State by Crouch JD shares their Top 10 Noise Rock Releases So Far This YearDoppler - Pourquoi ce disque ?In terms of sonic scope, compositional prowess, and progressive approaches, few noise rock releases this year have stood up to Pourquoi ce disque ? by Doppler. It’s true that Mandy, Indiana’s newest is one of the most sonically innovative and unsettling noise rock albums I’ve heard in a while, and, if I’m being honest, Zu’s take on noise rock is actually complex hard prog with a healthy dose of dissonance. But I still can’t get over Doppler’s brilliant, labyrinthine songwriting. “Incipit Expicit” is an early example on their 2026 release, as the song transitions from swinging, odd-metered noise rock to post-punk reggae. The song then swerves into a lengthy, driving climax that gradually builds in tension before exploding into unbridled fury. Aside from the meticulously composed songs, the album has an emotional depth beyond the visceral anger prevalent on most noise rock albums. There is an air of Queens of the Stone Age-like playfulness during the closing solo in “Of Pieces of Break.” That track is juxtaposed against the subsequent ruminative restraint of instrumental “Piano Cassé,” which features a nearly meditative percussionless interplay between the guitar and bass for half of the song’s running time. These sonic and emotional explorations illustrate a musical ambition that makes Pourquoi ce disque ? one of the most engaging listens of the year, and not just within the noise rock genre. Pourquoi Ce Disque ? by DOPPLER Mandy, Indiana - URGHHammok - When Does This Place Become Our SceneBitter Branches - Let’s Give The Land Back To The AnimalsZu - Ferrum SidereumTruck Violence - The weathervane is my bodyBags Bags Bags - It Eats Me UpAPE AMP - APE AMPThe Freqs - No God on the Gold CoastParts & Labor - Set of All SetsTB Shares their Top 10 Screamo Releases So Far This YearOstraca - ThreadI'm not sure if it says more about this album or this year, but for the first time covering this genre there is an obvious number one album. Thread is another powerful release from one of the brightest names in the genre, showcasing a raw fury of violence and passion that coalesces into something beautiful in a way that is nearly unparalleled right now. Ostraca are a dynamic band, building off the strengths of bands like envy and city of caterpillar before them. However, while there's a similar sense of atmospheric tension-stretching, they double down on the heaviness. In their songwriting this often comes across as a “calm before the storm” of sorts, such as the eerily beautiful acoustic passages in “Song for November”, before exploding into distorted, earth-churning evolutions of those same riffs. They're effective at making these dense walls of heaviness feel earned, with thoughtful bridges which seamlessly carry their passion throughout each song. It’s refreshing when this doesn’t just feel reserved for when they're pushed to the brink. And it’s not just the vocals or the minor ambient riffing, but the way their songwriting brings it all together. If you’re looking for a gut punch of grief and emotional catharsis, it’s hard to find a better band to listen to right now. While generally lumped into the screamo realm, it’s difficult to define them due to their heavy post-metal influence. Not to mention they’re one of few bands in the scene to incorporate lower guttural vocals into their sound. If you’re more into the punk and emo side of the genre this might not be as much of your thing, but it’s hard to deny the transcendental impact of their emotional delivery. Listening to this album on a lengthy solo drive across northern Ontario, I found myself lost in a sort of cinematic nostalgic yearning. Like someone looking through a photo album in a dimly lit room, feeling a thread in your heart slowly start to pull. Somewhere between an existential depression and a pensive contemplation which builds into a fervorous fury. I had the pleasure of seeing Ostraca recently at New Friends Fest in Toronto and was happy to see that these emotions were equally conveyed in their live performance. It seemed to permeate through to the audience both in the softer moments, allowing the crowd to just sink in that weight, ready to erupt into chaos and emotive scream-alongs. An all-around frenzied, engaging and cathartic experience that reflects the essence of their music.  Thread by ostraca Eyelet - SolenoidCassus - Scalis FeldenChalk Hands - The Line That Shapes the Coast of UsThe Saddest Landscape - Alone with HeavenKnumears - DirectionsQuiet Fear - La tierra arriba / El abismo abajoHouse of the Blood Choir - Mom’s AnxietySnag - All the Cages Holding Us Will One Day Turn to DustGros Enfant Mort - Le Sang Des PierresAs Living Arrows - Fragment IJD shares their Top 10 Grindcore Releases So Far This Year (Including Powerviolence, Deathgrind, Mathgrind, Noisegrind, Goregrind, Cybergrind, and Fake Grind)Eastwood - Alle Gegen AlleIn my view, grindcore perfection is often a matter of striking a balance. Too often, grind bands of various stripes end up at one extreme or the other regarding compositions, performances, and production quality. Some overcomplicate songs with endless noodling, whereas others often keep it caveman simple. Some employ an overly clinical approach to production in which the perfectly quantized performances sound lifeless. Some have subpar production values with sloppy performances. In a genre predicated on extremes, this shouldn’t be too surprising; but, in my humble opinion, the sweet spot is when bands strike a balance between those extremes. Eastwood’s Alle Gegen Alle is the best example of this so far this year. The German quartet’s second full-length is full of tightly performed, technically impressive blasts of grindcore coupled with a crystal-clear mix in which the humanness of the performances shines through. The compositions are dense without being overwrought. They rapidly cycle through changes that barely allow the listener to keep their footing, such as the blast-and-mosh tradeoff at the end of “Im Namen des Gehetztes”. But the compositions contain more than enough meat for the listener to chew on, especially as slower tempos and melodic elements peak through from time to time and add some variety, such as in “Alle Gegen Alle” and “Dampfgegart,” respectively. However, the majority of the 11-minute album is, on the whole, visceral and unforgiving. Oh, and did I mention that there is an Assück cover? items._cn_summary: Kelela的第三张专辑由奥斯卡·谢勒几乎全程参与制作，呈现出兼具锐利边缘与深邃质感的声响，同时旋律上具有较高的亲和力，使原本偏地下气质的风格转向更直接的流行表达。PinkPantheress与A.K. Paul的客串为作品增添了话题性，整体听感在实验电子与当代R&B之间取得平衡。专辑在保持个人辨识度的同时，也显露出向更广泛听众靠拢的意图。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A project that Al Kooper supported and saw to publication after he left Blood Sweat & Tears: songs that "fell out of the head of" 19-year old guitarist and singer-songwriter, John Parker Compton and his three Boston-based collaborators/friends. It was the first time in a New York City recording studio (Columbia) for all four of the young musicians. One amplifier. One violin and one cello with no overdubs. No original percussion instrument, just a 17-year old bass player. 1. "Tulu Rogers" (3:57) a folk song that feels quite like an early DONOVAN song when it's just John Parker and his guitar. Once his strings companions join in there is the feeling as if an entire section of orchestra strings has joined in--and yet there is also a strong charge of Rock 'n' Roll energy being channeled by the simple music as well. This is a song that I feel could/would've been quite popular with the lyrics-driven public. (9/10)2. "Thoughts For Polly" (5:48) gentle acoustic guitar folk music which is enhanced from the start by alto saxophone, electrified harpsichord, and Country-Western drumming. A very powerful, haunting, and poetic song that is greatly augmented by the contributions of the strings and "weird" (the recorded tape being played backwards) saxophone notes. Though this is by far the album's longest song, it exudes such a comforting vibe that it feels just right--a welcome balm from start to finish. A top three song for me. (9.125/10)3. "Feathers" (2:27) two arpeggiated guitar chords set the stage for the joinder of John Parker's chamber strings companions (as well as Al Kooper's guitar and Artie Schreck's sensitive drums). The vocal performance, style, and lyrics give the song a feel of something between the gentle side of Mick Jagger (think "As Tears Go By") and Jim Croce. (9/10)4. "Bi-Weekly" (3:33) opening with a little of the Baroque pep of a Burt Bacharach or Jimmy Webb tune, oboe, organ, drums, and full orchestra support continue to launch this wonderful vocal into the realm of those two master composers. Awesome chord shift into the wonderful chorus. Another top three song. (9.125/10)5. "Glossolalia" (4:06) open sea sounds like seagulls and waves open this one before John Parker and his string quartet join in with Bobby Colomby's percussion, Al Kooper's Vibraphone play, and Tony Ackerman's additional guitar to create the gentle folk music to back John Parker's near-talking Van Morrison-like vocal performance. I don't particularly like this vocal styling but I love the mood set up by the beautiful music. (9/10) 6. "Rivers Run To The Sea" (3:30) uptempo folk-rock music that sets up a Gordon Lightfoot/Jim Croce/AL STEWART-like vocal performance. After 90 seconds in one motif, the music slows down and becomes much more intentional for its chorus, but then the horse hooves and violin pick back up to return to the verse motif. So like Al Stewart! An awesome composition rendered beautifully. (9.125/10)7. "Pascal's Paradox" (3:21) a song that Al allowed to remain untouched the way John Parker and his quartet had originally arranged it. Sounds a lot like Jim Croce's "I Got a Name." Were I into lyrics this song might have earned higher marks from me; as it is it's a nice little Baroque Chamber Pop Folk tune.(8.75/10)8. "Yesterday's Roads" (3:19) opening with the two strings players before guitar, bass, drums, and "toy" piano (upper register) join in with John Parker's Dylan-like vocal. The music plays out like something from a jazzier yet-melancholic realm--like something by Phoebe Snow, Gordon Lightfoot or Roddy Frame (Aztec Camera)--or, from the modern day, Alisdair MacLean (The Clientele) or the late Nick Talbot (Gravenhurst) and so many other "sensitive" singer-songwriters. (8.875/10)9. "Now That I Want You" (2:32) the most animated song on the album is ramped up to Brit Rock standards by the contribution of Charlie Calello's full orchestra. (8.667/10)10. "Georgia Street" (4:44) a song that is enhanced by guest appearances from Al on electric piano, Blood, Sweat & Tears drummer, Bobby Colomby, and, later in the song, Fred Lipsius' saxophone, this Chamber Folk song achieves the amazing feat of replicating with uncanny accuracy a Moody Blues-like Mellotron with just two strings players! Very cool final minute. (9.125/10)11. "Rosalie" (4:28) reminds me of a cross between Jim Croce, early Elton John, and The Rolling Stones. (8.875/10)Total time 41:45Al's reverence for artists like Bob Dylan, The Band, The Allman Brothers, and The Rolling Stones really shines through with the production and enhancements he added to John Parker's original tracks. B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of wonderfully-precocious Baroque Chamber Pop Folk gently and masterfully nurtured and produced by Columbia Records via up-and-coming musical catalyst Al Kooper.
items._cn_summary: 这张1969年的专辑由Al Kooper支持完成，四位年轻音乐人在纽约哥伦比亚录音室录制，仅用一台放大器、一把小提琴和一把大提琴，无叠录，也没有传统打击乐，由17岁贝斯手支撑节奏。音乐以民谣为基底，融合弦乐四重奏、萨克斯、大键琴、管风琴及反向磁带效果，呈现出介于民谣摇滚与早期前卫之间的声响。歌曲结构常从轻柔民谣段落转向更具戏剧性的合唱，人声风格接近Donovan、Jim Croce或Van Morrison。整体上作品带有60年代末的创作歌手气质，编曲精致但实验性有限，属于前卫摇滚萌芽期的温和样本。

items.body: Review by HogweedOfTuscany — I'm no stranger to controversy, but in a world full of internet contrarians and outright trolling, I feel obligated to particularly explain why this album - possibly the most well-known prog album, with immaculate sales and even more immaculate production and famous cover, the album that would make Pink Floyd not only a household name, but classic rock legends on its own - gets the measly three stars from me. Especially as back in secondary school, Pink Floyd used to be my favourite band, after taking the torch from Led Zeppelin - and despite "getting" Floyd as much as a fan can, I honestly had trouble with the general adoration even back then. How dare I? Well, let's see.I'll start with the obvious - there is way too little actual musical ideas on this album. Before you bring out your pitchforks, just count with me - Speak to Me is a short amusical collage, Breathe is a very nice acoustic shuffle that A. isn't really a finished song as such, B. is nonetheless repeated three times over the course of the relatively short album with variations that don't really make it deserved, On the Run is more or less a half-musical failed experiment (I realise it's supposed to support the concept - which I'll get to later - being a psychological embodiment of the hectic modern world, anxiety and paranoia, but the execution itself is severely lacking - Waters would get much better at these "psychology first" unpleasant electronic detours on the latter albums, like with Welcome to the Machine), Time is great, but VERY similar to Breathe (to the level of me not even recognising when the song shifted into the Breathe Reprise on my first listen), Great Gig in the Sky, whether you like it or not, is more or less an unstructured, gospellish vocal performance (that more or less stands or falls on the shoulders of the vocalist), Eclipse is just an outro to Brain Damage that doesn't really deserve being considered a separate song and that leaves us with four finished, complete songs on the album: Time, Money, Us and Them and Brain Damage. Of these, Money switches its great flow and rhythm into a frankly somewhat pedestrian jamming session (I mean, I have collected Floyd bootlegs and loved their solos and such, but this one doesn't feel particularly inspired), Us and Them (despite being my second favourite off the record) is way too overlong for such a slow-trodding funeral dirge on a second half of the album, Brain Damage annoys me for reasons I'll get into in the next paragraph and Time feels way too lethargic for a song that's the definite highlight of the album. But I suppose my biggest issue with the album is that it's too... approachable. It doesn't really dabble in poetry, in anything even slightly highbrow, it does away with allegory and just confronts you with the ideas and the concept, with all the power and all the grace of a small-town thinker. "Too didactic" is probably the word that came to mind most, on this most recent listen. You're being told and explained and preached to by Roger Waters (who certainly isn't the person to be doing so) what he doesn't like about the world this time and how you should approach your life accordingly. Without any subtlety or nuance, in the great tradition of Bob Dylan around cca 1964. This honestly makes all the concessions to the concept of the album even worse, because this higher purpose is eventually somewhat disappointing. "But hey, Hogweed," you say, "don't you also often complain about the times prog bands were way TOO obtuse and too much detached from reality, crawled up their own intestine, like with The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway?" Well, yes, neither extreme is preferable, honestly, but one is certainly more artful than the other. But I understand that the honestly unimaginable commercial success was also caused by this, much like by Parson's production and so on. But to me, it's way too little, delivered in a somewhat underwhelming way primarily by a person who certainly shouldn't be in the position of a guru, though his descent into the Everbile was yet to come on the following albums. And taking itself way too seriously, with an undeserved weight. But I admit that the sentence "Hanging on in quiet desperation is the English way" is great and hilarious. And that brings us to my third concern, that is, some genuinely baffling decisions, especially regarding the general atmosphere and tonal coherence. Putting the most acerbic and sarcastic song Money into the mouth of Gilmour, with his inherent vocal wistfulness and melancholy, feels really weird (through a modern lens, it kinda gives off the vibe of the "old man yelling a cloud", he's just spitting the words "New car, caviar, four star daydream // Think I'll buy me a football team" but he overdoes it with the nonchalance, sounding more confused than anything). The jams don't really leave an impression on me, they're not nostalgic, they're not mindful, they're just as lethargic as the rest of the album. Nice, but really not outstanding. And Great Gig... while realising I'm probably going to make myself some new enemies now, I don't really like the song, nor do I understand the enthrallment that it elicits in so many people. I am quite well-versed in American soul music (from Otis Redding and Sam Cooke to Aretha and Diana Ross), I understand its appeal, but A. I find the combination with Floyd's particular English jazzy melancholy really doesn't work for me, and it sticks out from the album like a sore thumb, B. honestly, I just dislike Clare Torry's vocals, the timbre, the overwrought histrionics of it all. I realise that's just me and that I might be the only person in the world to find the performance more grating than anything, but especially as an artistic representation of death and the afterlife, probably the highest concept the album ever aspires to, it's way off the mark for me, all the more since it's positioned more or less as the centrepiece of the album.Not to drown too much in a sea of negativity - don't want to end up like Waters, after all - the things that really work about this album REALLY work, and I can see very well how the DSOTM mirage can captivate the listener. All the flaws I mentioned above, despite being really hard to stomach for me, are exceptionall well hidden. You don't really notice that they've been revisiting Breathe for the third time once they start their elevator jam in Any Colour You Like - not at first, at least. The heartbeats, the spoken snippets, the general flow and the audio quality, the catchy 7/8 of Money - it does give off the vibe of the lads being so apparently pleased with themselves were more or less justified. There are famous works of art that deserve its stature way less. So ignore the lyrics and raise my rating to four stars. Or go listen to Wish You Were Here and Animals.

items._cn_summary: 乐评认为这张专辑虽制作精良、封面著名，但实际音乐想法匮乏，仅四首完整歌曲，其余为拼贴或实验片段。Breathe多次变体重现，On the Run被指为失败的半音乐实验，Great Gig in the Sky被视作依赖歌手的无结构表现。概念主题过于直白说教，缺乏诗意与隐喻，整体显得过于平易近人。尽管Time和Us and Them等曲目有亮点，但结构松散、篇幅冗长，削弱了艺术冲击力。乐评者承认其历史地位，但认为其创新性与深度不足，与前卫摇滚的探索精神有所偏离。

items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑记录了Dr. John于1999年在德国Loreley露天剧场的演出，由新奥尔良乐手组成的四重奏伴奏。曲目包括《Iko Iko》《Qualified》《I Walk on Guilded Splinters》等标志性作品，融合了Mardi Gras游行节奏、放克律动、布鲁斯与摇滚元素，并加入对Duke Ellington的放克化改编。演出风格强调即兴互动与仪式感，歌词涉及神秘主义与巫毒意象，但整体仍属于传统新奥尔良根源音乐的范畴，缺乏实验性或前卫性的突破。作为现场档案，它呈现了Dr. John成熟期的舞台魅力与文化根基，适合对该风格感兴趣的听众，但与用户偏好的实验、爵士或电子方向关联较弱。

items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于实验作曲家泰永代·布雷克斯顿专辑的反向评测式导读。原文将他近作定位为完整的"反专辑"——并非传统意义上的长篇唱片，而更像是一场对唱片格式本身的拆解与否定。从有限的文字信息来看，作者试图传达的是作品在结构与呈现方式上的反常规态度，强调其跳出线性聆听逻辑的姿态。Brexton 作为来自先锋音乐世家的作曲家，其创作常涉及电子手段、声音装置与即兴元素的综合运用。本次作品显然延续了他对音乐边界与听觉经验之间关系的持续追问，但由于正文仅提供极短摘要，缺乏具体声音描述、创作手法分析或作品内部展开方式的讨论，实际可获取的信息密度极低，无法对作品本身做出更为深入的评价。

items.body: The Proms concert on August 10 was presented by an orchestra consisting of students from the Juilliard School in New York and the Royal Academy of Music, conducted by Esa-Pekka Salonen, with Vilde Frang as violin soloist. The program consisted of works by three of the most imporant composers of the early twentieth century, Igor Stravinsky (Symphony in Three Movements, 1942-45), Alban Berg (Violin Concerto, 1935, and Béla Bartok, Concerto for Ochestra, 1943-rev 1945). The Stravinsky, written after his move to California is a reaction not only to the ongoing world war (the program notes quoted Stravinsky in one of his conversation books with Robert Craft saying that the third movement was a ‘musical reaction to the newsreels and documentaries that I had seen of goose-stepping soldiers”) but his relations with business in his new home (the second movement began as sketches for possible music for the movie of Werfel’s The Song of Bernadette). This listener, on hearing the first movement, was reminded of a quote from W. H. Auden that sometimes the mature poet will have need to imitate himself, since it seemed to be a perfect imitation of a Stravinsky piece. The Berg Concerto, on the other hand is completely first hand, and genuine. The performance was somewhat lacking in terms of its shaping and balancing. The Albert Hall can be especially difficult for a soloist in terms of playing to the hall and that is especially true of the Berg. For this listener the most convincing performance was of the Bartok Concerto for Orchestra, It is certainly the most familiar of the three pieces, and that familiarity can cause it to be somewhat taken for granted. This performance made one realize what a very very good piece it is, and brought out all its strengths and, in fact, all of Bartok’s strengths. If one needed a comparison between a world class, absolutely beyond reproach student orchestra and a thoroughly ‘grown-up,” “professional” one, it was provided the next night by the Los Angeles Philharmonic. Conducted by its artistic director, Gustavo Dudamel. The concert began with a staggeringly beautiful performance of the Beethoven Pastorale Symphony, full of beauty of tone, nuance, color, and clarity of articulation and was followed by the first part of the ballet Dante by Thomas Adès, Inferno, the performance of which was equally brilliant. Dante is a score for a ballet by choreographer Wayne McGregory, a long-time collaborator of Adés. In the first part which was what was played on this concert, Adés uses music of Lizst in much the same way the Stravinsky used the music of Pergolesi in his ballet Pulcinella. Various works of Lizst constitute the content of the work, and can be quoted and orchestrated, but also can be used as source material for music less directly related to specific pieces. The first twelve sections of the work, tracing the circles of hell, build energy leading up to the rousing (described by Venn as showstopping) the Theives, which the audience assumed was the finale, and cheered enthuisatically when it ended. However there was a final circle, Satan, depicting Lucifer trapped in ice, which brought the piece to a conclusion which might well be described as bone chilling. All of the work is brilliantly conceived and realized, with fabulous orchestration, and awesome instrumental writing. To be completely honest, it left this listener a little cold. The audience loved it. The concert by the Los Angeles Philharmonic was followed by a late-night Prom given by Evelyn Glennie, the BBC Singers, and the Fantasia Orchestra, conducted by Tom Fetherstonehaugh. There wass also sign language interpretation by Sean Chandler. There was a very wide range of types and styles of music; Glennie, in an interview in the program, described the programming strategy as being like ‘walking through different rooms of human experience.’ The program started with John Coltrane’s Welcome, followed by It Don’t Mean a Thing by Duke Ellington. It went on from there to include music by Morton Feldman (some of Rothko Chapel), Caroline Shaw, Dvorak, Vaughan Williams (Serenade to Music), and Radiohead, including, along the way a piece by Glennie and Philip Sheppard, a first Prom performance of Sandman’s Castle by Vincent Ho, and a first performance of The Wood Pigeon by Héloïse Werner, commissioned by the BBC for this concert, ending up with Meredith Monk’s Panda Chant. The playing and singing by all concerned was wonderful and engaging and the whole experience was refreshing and exhilarating. items.body: The six tracks on “Decay” came out of the same sessions as “Purge” three years ago, and Justin Broadrick held them back while he looked for a label. He found one: the tenth Godflesh album arrives on 25 September 2026 through Relapse Records, the first the Birmingham industrial duo have issued outside Broadrick’s own Avalanche Recordings since their 2010 return. “Living/Ending” is the first single. “Decay” is the penultimate Godflesh album, not the last one. Broadrick has said a further record is written and still to be recorded, and in March 2026 he announced the end of Godflesh live performances after abdominal surgery for a hernia. Broadrick explained where the record came from and why it took three years to surface: “Decay was born from the same sessions as Purge,” he stated. “It was one huge pool of songs. I picked what I felt was appropriate for what I wanted to achieve with Purge, with the intention of releasing the songs that didn’t fit as a new album within a year of Purge being released. Unfortunately, two years passed whilst considering external labels, so that I didn’t have to self-release GODFLESH anymore, but it took an awful lot of time to establish a comfortable home for me. The recordings were done, but as usual for me, I did change a lot of stuff once I came back to it.” The band have done this before. “Decline & Fall”, issued on 2 June 2014, was built the same way, from tracks Broadrick cut from the sessions that produced “A World Lit Only By Fire” four months later. He also addressed how the surgery intersected with the recording, since the hernia itself came from the way he sings: “Fortunately, all of the recordings for Decay were completed long before the surgery, vocals included… although the back end of a couple of songs were recorded with the hernia itself, and that was a struggle. I was already aware that the GODFLESH shout, so to speak, was exacerbating the hernia greatly, as was every GODFLESH performance in the lead-up to the surgery once the hernia appeared, and the hernia was mostly caused by year upon year of shouting in GODFLESH. The album was mixed post-surgery, and while I was still in some pain and considerable discomfort, but fortunately GODFLESH is generally me expressing my pain, albeit [usually] mental, philosophical and existential, whereas this was physical pain.” Broadrick points to the opening and closing tracks as the record’s core, and notes that the two of them together run half its length: “The bookends of Decay are the most important pieces to me. They say it all, so to speak; the album could have been just those two songs alone – the duration of them is half of the total album!” Decay by GODFLESH Godflesh ‘Decay’ tracklist and formats The album runs six tracks: “Master and Slave” “Living/Ending” “Feral Colony” “Fear Of Man” “Fodder” “Consume Me” Relapse Records offers “Decay” on 12-inch vinyl, CD and cassette, with a digital edition through Bandcamp. A deluxe 12-inch pressing in two limited colours, housed in a silver board laminated jacket with gloss UV and packaged with a slipmat, poster and sticker, has already sold out at the label store. About Godflesh Justin Broadrick and bassist G.C. Green formed Godflesh in Birmingham, England, in 1988. Broadrick had played guitar on side one of Napalm Death’s “Scum” the year before, and the pair built Godflesh around downtuned guitar, bass and a drum machine rather than a live drummer. The self-titled debut EP arrived in 1988, followed by the album “Streetcleaner” on Earache Records on 13 November 1989. “Pure” came in 1992. The band ran until 2002, when Broadrick ended the project during a US tour; “Hymns”, from 2001, was the last album of that period. He spent the following years on Jesu and other projects before reactivating Godflesh in 2010 with Green. The reunion output came out on Broadrick’s own Avalanche Recordings. The “Decline & Fall” EP appeared on 2 June 2014 and the seventh album, “A World Lit Only By Fire”, on 7 October 2014. “Post Self” followed in October 2017 on vinyl and CD. Six years later the duo returned with the ninth album “Purge” on 9 June 2023, previewed by “the ‘Nero’ single and a US tour announcement”. Away from Godflesh, Broadrick records as JK Flesh and has remixed and contributed to work by acts including Pitchshifter and Derision Cult, the latter alongside members of Ministry and The Cure. “Decay” leaves one Godflesh album still to record. On what closing the project means, Broadrick stated: “It expresses my pain, and I’ve put my body and soul into this expression for the majority of my existence. I feel quite lucky, because Godflesh is now physically impossible for me, rendering it useless. I now wish to move out of its constraints, move on creatively with heavy/ugly music to new ground.”
items._cn_summary: 这篇文章实质上是一篇新闻稿而非乐评，详细报道了Godflesh第十张专辑《Decay》的发行信息：六首曲目源自三年前《Purge》的同期录音，2026年9月25日由Relapse Records发行，这是乐队自2010年复出以来首次在Avalanche Recordings之外的厂牌发行作品。文章还透露主唱Justin Broadrick因疝气手术宣布终止Godflesh现场演出，并解释了录音期间身体疼痛如何影响创作过程。首支单曲为《Living/Ending》，专辑首尾两首曲目合计占整张专辑一半时长，被Broadrick视为核心。整体内容以新闻事实陈述为主，缺乏对音乐本身的深度评论或听觉分析。

items.body: Los Angeles duo Zeistencroix self-released their album “Psychotronic” on August 14, 2026. The eight tracks run 29 minutes and 34 seconds and mix industrial rock guitars with electronic textures and alternative metal rhythms. Ulrich Wild, whose credits include Pantera, Deftones, Static-X, White Zombie and Powerman 5000, mixed and mastered seven of the songs and recorded the vocals at his own studio. The opener “Get It On” was mixed in Germany by Christoph Wieczorek of Annisokay, who has also worked with Eisbrecher. The record was tracked across studios in Los Angeles and Miami, with “Get It On” recorded at Stygian Sound by Alex Crescioni. The running order is “Get It On”, “Subliminal Intentions”, “Blame The One Behind”, “Deceiving”, “Decadence”, “Animals In Denial”, “So Long” and “My Love”. The release is digital and streaming; no physical edition has been announced and the album is not on Bandcamp. What Zeistencroix built ‘Psychotronic’ around Vocalist and guitarist Orlando “OD” Draven places the record in the present rather than in science fiction. He stated: “This is not an album about a dystopian future, it is about the moments that precede one.” On the themes he added: “Its themes are rooted in the present, exploring the social, political, and psychological shifts that can become the early symptoms of authoritarianism. It examines how fear, crisis, and division can normalize the gradual expansion of control over speech, thought, and personal autonomy, often before society recognizes the consequences.” Draven closes on the point the title carries: “Ultimately it’s a reminder that the future is not predetermined, and that recognizing the warning signs is the first step in preventing them from becoming permanent.” Drummer Santi Rivillas described the material as a step on from the band’s previous work, saying the songs are “heavier in some ways and more atmospheric in others”. About Zeistencroix Zeistencroix are a Los Angeles duo built around Orlando “OD” Draven on vocals, guitars and songwriting and Santi Rivillas on drums. Draven was born in Caracas and Rivillas comes from Miami. The pair describe their sound as post-industrial rock, drawing on industrial rock, alternative metal, electronic music and noir imagery. The project’s first release was the five-track EP “Gemini” on November 2, 2017, self-released and produced by Tim Palmer and Bill Metoyer, engineered by Alex Crescioni and mastered by Paul Abbott. The full-length “Gen Z” followed on October 1, 2019 through the Italian label Sliptrick Records, an eleven-song CD produced by Crescioni and Draven and preceded by the single “Sick” in July 2019. A live album recorded at Radio Artifact, “Zeistencroix Live 2021 06 27”, appeared in January 2022, and the five-track EP “Cruxi-Fiction” arrived on August 26, 2022 through Pavement Entertainment, produced by Tim Palmer, Alex Crescioni and Draven. The band toured the US West Coast behind it and later played a run as direct support to Crazy Town, alongside Los Angeles club dates including the Whisky a Go Go. “Psychotronic” is the first Zeistencroix record to carry no label at all, and the first to be built around outside mixers rather than a single in-house production team. It is also the project’s first appearance in Side-Line.

items._cn_summary: Zeistencroix是由洛杉矶双人组合推出的专辑《Psychotronic》，全长不到半小时，收录八首作品，融合工业摇滚吉他、电子音色与另类金属节奏。制作方面，七首曲目由曾与Pantera、Deftones、Static-X合作的Ulrich Wild混音及母带处理，开篇曲则由德国制作人Christoph Wieczorek完成。主唱兼词曲作者Orlando Draven阐述专辑主题聚焦于当下社会、政治与心理层面的变化，探讨威权主义如何在恐惧与分裂中被逐步合法化，并非指向虚构的末世场景。鼓手Santi Rivillas表示作品比以往更重也更具氛围感。整体定位为后工业摇滚，仅提供数字发行，无实体版本。

items.body: Two days before the album lands, Black Marble has released a video for “It Always Comes to Me”, the last advance single from “Life in Small Spaces”. The fifth Black Marble album arrives on 21 August 2026 through Sacred Bones Records on CD and on transparent orange vinyl. Claes Nordwall directed the video. Chris Stewart, the project’s sole member since 2016, follows the release with a North American tour opening on 22 August in Santa Ana, California. “It Always Comes to Me” opens the record. Stewart explains the song as a study of somebody who keeps getting away with things: “It Always Comes to Me is about a cool, calm, collected person who seems to always be able to get away with things other people can’t, either by charm or deceit,” he stated. “Like a modern version of The Kinks’ Dedicated Follower of Fashion, the song doesn’t explicitly advocate for or condemn this kind of behaviour, but takes a birds eye view of it as the protagonist moves through the world. Ultimately, it leaves it up to the listener to judge for themselves. The subject of the song seems to be having fun but can it last? And how much does our judgement really matter either way?” Bass and guitar carry more of the arrangement here than the layered synthesizers of earlier Black Marble records. Stewart has described what he wanted from the album’s guitar parts as an attempt to “create this chime-y hypnotic quality. Like a radio dial that is between two stations.” Nordwall filmed Stewart moving through New York subways, bridges, basketball courts and pool halls. The director connected that pacing to Finnish cinema: “I was drawn to the idea of a character moving through the modern world on his own timeline,” he stated. “While everything around him races forward, he remains quietly rooted in who he is. I was inspired by Chris’s ideas behind the album which made me think of the dry stoicism of Aki Kaurismäki’s films. I wanted to make something that celebrates resilience, character and the beauty of refusing to chase the next thing.” Life in Small Spaces by Black Marble “Life in Small Spaces” runs eleven tracks across two sides. Side one holds “It Always Comes To Me”, “Jim Carol New Year”, “Anything”, “Get Back Up”, “Other Man’s Dream” and “Guess”. Side two holds “Life Without”, “Missing History”, “Panopticon Calls”, “Picture When” and “Sonny Boy”. Side-Line covered the earlier single from the album when Black Marble shared “Anything” and set “Life in Small Spaces” on 18 July 2026. Black Marble tour dates for 2026 The tour runs from 22 August to 19 September 2026. The Serfs and Public Circuit open selected dates, with Jimmy Cicero on some shows. 22 August – Santa Ana, CA, USA – Constellation Room at the Observatory 23 August – Los Angeles, CA, USA – 1720 25 August – San Francisco, CA, USA – Rickshaw Stop 26 August – Sacramento, CA, USA – Harlow’s 28 August – Seattle, WA, USA – The Crocodile 29 August – Portland, OR, USA – Wonder Ballroom 30 August – Boise, ID, USA – Shrine Social Club 31 August – Salt Lake City, UT, USA – Urban Lounge 1 September – Denver, CO, USA – The Federal Theatre 3 September – Omaha, NE, USA – Slowdown 4 September – Minneapolis, MN, USA – Fine Line 5 September – Chicago, IL, USA – Thalia Hall 6 September – Detroit, MI, USA – El Club 7 September – Toronto, ON, Canada – Lee’s Palace 8 September – Montreal, QC, Canada – La Sala Rosa 10 September – New York City, NY, USA – Webster Hall 11 September – Philadelphia, PA, USA – Union Transfer 12 September – Baltimore, MD, USA – Ottobar 14 September – Raleigh, NC, USA – Kings 15 September – Atlanta, GA, USA – The Earl 17 September – Houston, TX, USA – White Oak Music Hall Upstairs 18 September – Dallas, TX, USA – Club Dada 19 September – Austin, TX, USA – 29th Street Ballroom About Black Marble Chris Stewart started Black Marble in Brooklyn in 2011 with Ty Kube of Team Robespierre. Sub Pop imprint Hardly Art signed the project after Stewart posted a single song online, and the debut album “A Different Arrangement” appeared on 9 October 2012. The second album, “It’s Immaterial”, followed in October 2016 on Ghostly International and marked Kube’s exit, leaving Stewart as the sole member. Stewart moved to Sacred Bones Records and relocated from Brooklyn to Los Angeles around the third album, “Bigger Than Life”, released on 25 October 2019. The covers EP “I Must Be Living Twice” came in August 2020 with reworkings of songs originally by Wire, Robert Palmer and Grouper. A fourth full-length, “Fast Idol”, arrived on 22 October 2021, also on Sacred Bones. “Anything”, issued on 17 July 2026 with a video by Scott Kiernan, previewed “Life in Small Spaces” a month before release. “It Always Comes to Me” closes the run-up to the album’s arrival on 21 August 2026 and the tour that starts the following day.
items._cn_summary: Black Marble 第五张专辑《Life in Small Spaces》共收录十一首作品，由唯一的核心成员 Chris Stewart 操刀制作。这张作品相较于以往作品，贝斯与吉他在编曲中承担了更突出的比重，Stewart 形容他所追求的吉他质感如同在两台电台之间的调频——带有一种催眠式的嗡鸣感。开场曲探讨了一个似乎总能逃脱后果的人物，以冷静旁观的视角记录其行为轨迹，不作道德评判，将判断权留给听众。MV 导演 Claes Nordwall 从阿基·考里斯马基的电影美学汲取灵感，呈现主角在纽约地铁、篮球场与泳池等场景中穿行的画面，强调一种拒绝追赶时代的沉稳姿态。尽管侧标对吉他音色的探索有一定想法，但整体制作偏向独立摇滚与后朋克的常规框架，缺乏对声音边界的实质拓展。

items.body:
Happy Mondays’ "Pills ‘n’ Thrills and Bellyaches", originally released in 1990.

"Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches stands as a key document of the Madchester era, fusing indie rock with acid house rhythms and loose-limbed funk. Packed with defining cuts like ‘Step On’ and ‘Kinky Afro’, it captured the hedonistic pulse of dancefloors and Northern nightlife while pushing British alternative music into new territory.

Equal parts swagger and groove, the album’s genre-blurring approach helped shape the sound of the early ’90s and continues to echo through modern indie and electronic scenes. Remastered from the original Factory Records tapes and accompanied by new liner notes from James Brown, it remains a vivid snapshot of a scene at full tilt."

items.body: In his booklet interview with Michelle Assay for Lunaris, Bruce Liu discusses his fascination with the night and his inner world of sound. The program includes familiar works like Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata alongside pieces by Mompou, Cage, and Agnes Obel. Lunaris Amazon Presto Apple Liu notes that Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata anchors the curation. A major point of interest is Beethoven’s marking that the entire first movement be played without dampers (senza sordini). On a modern piano, this implies holding the damper pedal down continuously, an approach that can be problematic given the instrument’s resonance compared to a fortepiano. Liu’s pedaling remains clean throughout. While the Adagio sostenuto (track 2) leans toward the austere, it communicates the intended solemnity. The Allegretto is deliberate without becoming mannered in its elegance, while the Presto agitato (track 4) introduces the necessary intensity. Liu’s precise fingerwork prevents the textures from becoming oversaturated, and the subito accents drive the volatility and urgency central to the movement. Beethoven’s Sonata Op. 53 (Waldstein) serves as a thoughtful pairing with the Moonlight. The opening movement (track 8) captures the con brio spirit with tight articulation and clarity, and Liu’s decision to highlight select secondary voices adds dimension to the reading. The Introduzione (track 9) is calm, yet Liu uses moments of inflection toward its close to generate the suspense needed to connect to the final movement. The finale reflects the sonata’s L’Aurore nickname: Liu’s pedaling imparts the haze of dawn upon the opening theme (where Beethoven again asks for the pedal to be held). As the music reaches its climax, the textures become drier, resulting in an unusually crisp presentation. Scriabin’s Sonata No. 4 in F-sharp major (tracks 16-17) presents two distinct shades of anticipation. In the Andante, Liu demonstrates sensitivity and imagination, projecting a different tonal shade for each shifting harmony. This quiet yearning builds tension that is released in the Prestissimo volando. He navigates the rapid passages with precision and a certain lightness, the larger sections stay controlled without feeling subdued, and the movement’s trajectory of intensity is clearly shaped. While Debussy’s Clair de lune might seem an expected inclusion given the program’s theme, Liu opts instead for the composer’s Rêverie (track 5). From the hypnotic ostinato that opens the work, he builds a multicolored reading that alternates between lush and enigmatic textures. Across this range of expression, Liu’s bell-like tone maintains structural cohesion. Bruce Liu. Photo © Bartek Barczyk. Agnes Obel’s Tokka (track 7) is a meaningful addition in both genre and artistry. Through the music’s relative sparseness and concise phrases, Liu conveys transience and fragility. Similarly concise in phrasing, the first of Arnold Schoenberg’s 6 Kleine Klavierstücke, Op. 19 (track 14) offers an alternative perspective: Liu highlights the work’s angularity through a hushed tone, sharp articulation, and a persistent sense of enigma. Note that the Schoenberg, along with Reynaldo Hahn’s Hivernale, appears only on the digital and vinyl editions of the album; the CD omits both tracks. Liu takes a notable approach to the final work, John Cage’s Dream. Across the thrice-repeated material, he uses three different keyboards between two pianos (noting in the booklet that one instrument features two keyboards), and the effect is perceptible: each iteration has a distinct character, with the second sounding appropriately distant and murky. Throughout, Liu’s playing combines reflection, declamation, and meditation, emphasizing the structure of Cage’s minimalism. In a concept album of this nature, hearing directly from the artist is valuable. The detailed interview with Assay serves as an important companion to the program, presenting Liu as an introspective and articulate musician. His commentary aligns with performances that are insightful and reward a dedicated listen. items.body: Frank Zwicker and Klaus Schill began their journey as Sea Of Sin more than 30 years ago. Although the German duo released a remix album about two years ago, “The Shape Of A Lonely Soul” marks their first new studio album in seven years. The album was preceded by no fewer than four singles, which are joined here by four additional tracks to create a body of work largely inspired by inner struggles and the quest to break free from isolation in an ever-changing world. These are serious and profound themes on which to build Electro-Pop music. Yet Sea Of Sin achieves a delightful duality, balancing the gravity of the subject matter with an upbeat and joyful musical style. After all, music is meant to connect people, and perhaps this approach can help lonely souls emerge from isolation and reconnect with reality. Sea Of Sin retains its quintessential Electro-Pop sound, featuring catchy melodies and strong, memorable choruses. Add passionate vocal performances to the mix, and you get an enjoyable album that leaves you feeling better and happier. For me, the track “Dark Revelations” stands out in particular. It is simply a beautiful composition that would fit perfectly on a film Soundtrack. Sea Of Sin have returned with just eight tracks, but every single one of them is well worth a listen. (Rating:8). Listen to “Dark Revelations”: Dark Revelations by Sea of Sin About Sea Of Sin Sea Of Sin are a German new wave/pop duo from Hamburg built around founding members Frank Zwicker and Klaus Schill. The band first emerged in the 1990s and launched with the 1995 debut album “Watch Out!” on Subtronic Records. Zwicker handles vocals and lyrics, while Schill is responsible for synths, guitars and production. They followed in 1997 with the EP “Illuminate”, produced by Heiko Maile of Camouflage, who also handled arrangement, mastering and backing vocals on that release. “Urban Chemistry” arrived in 2000, with Maile again contributing backing vocals. After a long hiatus the duo returned in 2018 with “Future Pulse“, a comeback album largely built from re-edited earlier material. In April 2019 they issued “Unbroken”, described by the band as their first album of new songs after the break. Later that year came “The Remixes”, which collected remix work from the 2018-2019 period and added the previously unreleased track “Only The Memory Remains”. The release pace increased from 2020 onward with the singles “Unspoken Words”, “Floating Away”, “Turn Back Time” and “Immaculate”, gathered together with further remix work on “The Remixes II” in March 2021. The album “Tired of Chasing Ghosts” arrived on April 21, 2023. In 2024 the duo marked its 30-year anniversary with live dates. The singles “Faith!”, “No Excuse”, “Bang Bang Bang”, “Save Me”, “Renegades” and “Dark Revelations” led into “The Shape Of A Lonely Soul”, released on March 13, 2026. Klaus Schill handled mixing and production, Thomas Banse engineered the vocal recordings at Studio B in Stuttgart, and Norman Nitzsche mastered the record at Calyx Mastering in Berlin. The album is available as a CD digipak with a 16-page booklet, as a limited 12-inch black vinyl edition and digitally.

items.body: Yazoo, the English synthpop duo of Vince Clarke and Alison Moyet, released their debut album “Upstairs at Eric’s” on 20 August 1982 through Mute Records. The album turns 44 this year. It reached number two on the UK Albums Chart and was later certified platinum by the British Phonographic Industry. How Yazoo recorded ‘Upstairs at Eric’s’ The title points at Eric Radcliffe, who ran Blackwing Studios in London, where the sessions took place. Radcliffe produced the record with Yazoo and engineered it with John Fryer. Daniel Miller, the Mute founder who signed the duo, added production. Clarke wrote seven of the eleven tracks: “Don’t Go,” “Too Pieces,” “Bad Connection,” “I Before E Except After C,” “In My Room,” “Only You” and “Tuesday.” Moyet wrote the other four: “Midnight,” “Goodbye 70’s,” “Winter Kills” and “Bring Your Love Down (Didn’t I).” Two UK top-three singles, “Only You” and “Don’t Go,” had already charted before the album arrived. Clarke had left Depeche Mode after that band’s 1981 debut “Speak & Spell,” and the pair came together through an advertisement Moyet placed in Melody Maker. Moyet has described what she was looking for at the time: “I put an ad in Melody Maker looking for a semi-professional band […] Not someone who’d just had a massive hit album.” The two had known each other since their school years in Basildon, Essex. Clarke recalled taking the duo’s first recording to Miller, and getting a reading he misjudged: “I took the demo to Daniel Miller at Mute, and I got the distinct impression he was not interested. ‘That’s that,’ I thought. ‘Get a proper job’.” Clarke has described the sessions themselves as unplanned: “Nobody really knew what they were doing. We were open to trying anything – it was like being in a toy shop, finding out what would happen if you pressed different buttons.” In North America the album appeared under the name Yaz, on Sire Records. Mute issued a remastered edition in 2008, the version now on streaming services, alongside the “In Your Room” box set and the duo’s Reconnected tour. About Yazoo Yazoo formed in Basildon, Essex, in late 1981, with Clarke on keyboards and Moyet on vocals and piano. Mute released their first single, “Only You,” in May 1982; it reached number two on the UK Singles Chart. “Don’t Go” followed and entered the UK top five, and “Upstairs at Eric’s” arrived on 20 August 1982. The duo toured Britain that year as the Guided Tour, and in 1983 won the Brit Award for British Breakthrough Act alongside a nomination for British Group. The partnership did not survive the second album. Clarke and Moyet split in May 1983, before “You and Me Both” reached shops. Moyet began a solo career with “Alf” in 1984; Clarke co-founded The Assembly, then formed Erasure with Andy Bell in 1985. A quarter of a century later the two reconciled, reissuing both studio albums with the “In Your Room” box set and touring the UK, Europe and North America in 2008 as Reconnected, documented on the 2010 live album “Reconnected Live.” They shared a stage again in May 2011, performing three Yazoo songs at a festival organised by Mute. Side-Line has since covered Clarke’s first solo album in Vince Clarke launches debut solo album ‘Songs of Silence’ – Out now, the archive footage in The last Depeche Mode show with Vince Clarke – Watch it now, and a recent reworking of the duo’s final single in Yazoo hit ‘Nobody’s Diary’ gets Sgt Slick rework – Out now. Forty-four years on, “Upstairs at Eric’s” remains the first of the two albums the duo completed together.

items.body:
'I Bet on Sky' is the third Dinosaur Jr. album since the original trio – J Mascis, Lou Barlow and Murph – reformed in 2005 and it marks the band’s 10th studio album since their debut on Homestead Records in 1985. 

"Back in the ‘80s, if anyone has suggested that these guys would be performing and recording at such a high level 27 years later, they would have been laughed out of the tree fort.

The trio has taken everything they’ve learned from the various projects they tackled over the years, and poured it directly into their current mix. J’s guitar approaches some of its most unhinged playing here, but there’s a sense of instrumental control that matches the sweet murk of his vocals (not that he always remembers to exercise control on stage, but that’s another milieu). This is head-bobbing riff-romance at the apex. Lou’s basswork shows a lot more melodicism now as well, although his two songs on I Bet on Sky retain the jagged rhythmic edge that has so often marked his work. And Murph…well, he still pounds the drums as hard and as strong as a pro wrestler, with deceptively simple structures that manage to interweave themselves perfectly with his bandmates’ melodic explosions.

After submerging myself in I Bet on Sky, it’s clear that the album is a true and worthy addition to the Dinosaur Jr. discography. It hews close enough to rock formalism to please the squares. Yet it is brilliantly imprinted with the trio’s magical equation, which is a gift to the rest of us. For a combo that began as anomalous fusion of hardcore punk and pop influences, Dinosaur Jr. have proven themselves to be unlikely masters of the long game."

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Dinosaur Jr. 原班人马重组后的第三张录音室作品，也是乐队的第十张录音室专辑。乐评指出，乐队将多年积累的经验融入当前创作：J Mascis 的吉他演奏近乎失控但仍在器乐控制之内，与模糊人声形成平衡；Lou Barlow 的贝斯更具旋律性，同时保留锯齿般的节奏边缘；Murph 的鼓击依然沉重有力，结构看似简单却与乐队旋律爆发完美交织。专辑在摇滚形式主义框架内贴近传统，又印刻着乐队独特的魔力公式。作为从硬核朋克与流行影响异质融合而来的组合，Dinosaur Jr. 证明了他们擅长长期主义。

items.body: Sacramento dream pop group Soft Science released “Fade” on 18 August 2026, the third single taken from their fifth album “Sand”. The album arrives on 4 September 2026 on CD and vinyl through Shelflife Records in North America and Spinout Nuggets in the UK. “Fade” is on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music, and comes with an official video. Fade by Soft Science The six-piece mix dream pop, shoegaze and indie rock, with Katie Haley’s vocals over twin guitars, bass, drums and electronics. “Fade” sets a four-on-the-floor pulse against a slower vocal line, with a guitar figure from Matt Levine on the bridge and harmonies from Haley across the verses. Haley points to the tension in the arrangement as the reason the track went onto the album early. “This was one of the first song ideas Ross came up with for the album. I was immediately drawn to the core of the song as it is ethereal pop but, at the same time, it has a driving force,” she said, adding: “When I was coming up with the lyrics, I imagined this song playing in the car on a romanticized road trip, driving along the coast or something like that. This is one of our favorites to play live from “Sand”; we all picked it up really easily and it has an energy that feels good to perform.” Ross Levine traces the opening lyric back to a phrase he overheard. “Matt’s guitar line on the bridge and Katie’s harmony on the verses are some of the high points on this track. The lyrical inspiration for the first line, “foreign lands”, was from something I heard someone say: “The past is a foreign country”. I thought the concept was really interesting,” he said. What ‘Fade’ adds to the Soft Science album ‘Sand’ “Fade” is the third track on “Sand” and the third single lifted from it, after “Spinning” in June 2026 and “Understand” in July. The ten-track running order is “Spinning”, “Go”, “Fade”, “Without”, “Sand”, “Everything”, “Thread”, “Understand”, “Hope” and “Sway”. The band recorded the album at Shattered Records and The Pool House, with Jack O’Donnell engineering and additional engineering by Ross Levine. Kev Bolus mixed it at OneEleven and Antony Ryan mastered it at Red Red Paw. Soft Science produced the record themselves; John Conley supplied the artwork. Lyrics are credited to Katie Haley and Ross Levine, with the songs written by Haley, Ross Levine, Matt Levine, Becky Cale and Tony Cale, and Hans Munz added as co-writer on “Thread”, “Without” and “Sway”. About Soft Science Soft Science formed in Sacramento, California in 2009 around Katie Haley and the brothers Ross and Matt Levine. The current line-up is Haley on lead vocals and percussion, Matt Levine on lead guitar, Ross Levine on guitar, synths and backing vocals, Becky Cale on bass and backing vocals, Tony Cale on drums and Hans Munz on electronics. The band self-released its first three albums: “Highs and Lows” in 2011, “Detour” in 2013 and “Maps” in 2018. A split 7-inch with The Luxembourg Signal appeared in 2015, and 2018 also brought a pair of covers, The House of Love’s “I Don’t Know Why I Love You” and Northern Picture Library’s “Paris”. The fourth album, “Lines”, came out in 2023 and was the group’s first release through Shelflife Records and Spinout Nuggets; Side-Line covered its lead single in “Kerosene” that August. Away from records, the band has recorded sessions for KEXP, WFMU and Part-Time Punks, and played New York Popfest, Paris Popfest, The Big Takeover’s 35th anniversary show, Schellraiser Festival, Tremolo Fest and Dreamgaze PDX, alongside shows in the United States and Europe. “Fade” is their third single of 2026, ahead of “Sand” on 4 September.

items.body:
Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以1819年彼得卢屠杀为背景，用原创歌曲结合当代民谣编曲，讲述英国工人运动史上的关键事件。Sean Cooney与Eliza Carthy、Sam Carter、Jennifer Reid等音乐人合作，以小型乐队编制营造出集会时的期待、冲突中的恐慌以及事后的哀伤。歌曲聚焦于萨姆·班福德、玛丽·菲尔德斯等具体人物的个人经历，也通过组曲刻画士兵的傲慢。专辑以书本形式附带信件、政治漫画和插图，构成多媒体叙事。整体上属于传统英国民谣叙事风格，音乐本身缺乏实验性或跨界融合元素，更接近历史题材的当代民谣创作。
